For this reason, the key question is how research is carried out. Responsible researchers follow the principle of using animals only when no alternative exists, using as few as possible and reducing pain through good care and anaesthesia. Research for trivial purposes, such as testing cosmetics, is much harder to justify than research for treating serious diseases.

In conclusion, using animals in medical research is a difficult moral question with no perfect answer. It is acceptable when the aim is to save human lives, when no alternative exists and when strict rules protect animals from unnecessary suffering. As better alternatives develop, its use should steadily decrease.

prompt: Some people think shops should sell everything at fixed prices. Others prefer the tradition of bargaining.
task: Discuss both views and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the advantages of fixed prices: fairness, speed, trust, protection for less confident buyers
Explains the advantages of bargaining: flexibility, tradition, relationships, benefit for skilled buyers and small sellers
Notes the disadvantages of each, such as overcharging tourists or loss of flexibility
Gives a clear personal opinion
Uses everyday market examples
Concludes clearly
model:
In many Pakistani bazaars, the price of a shawl or a pair of shoes is the beginning of a conversation, not the end. The shopkeeper names a figure, the customer offers half, and after some friendly argument they agree somewhere in between. Modern stores, by contrast, print a price on every tag. Which system is better? I believe fixed prices are fairer for most goods, though bargaining still has a place.

Supporters of fixed prices value fairness. Everyone pays the same, whether they are confident or shy, local or visiting, young or old. Customers do not have to worry about being cheated, and shopping becomes quicker and less stressful. Fixed prices also build trust: if a shop's prices are clearly displayed, customers can compare them with other shops and return confidently.

Supporters of bargaining argue that it is part of our culture and makes shopping social. A regular customer and a shopkeeper who have bargained for years often become friends. Bargaining gives flexibility: a seller can offer a discount to clear old stock or to help a customer who cannot afford the full price. Skilled bargainers can save a good deal of money.

Each system has drawbacks. Bargaining favours those who are confident and experienced, while others, such as tourists, students or people unfamiliar with a market, may pay far more than the item is worth. It also wastes time, especially for small purchases. Fixed prices, on the other hand, may be set high to begin with, and customers lose the chance to negotiate a better deal.

In my opinion, fixed prices should be the normal practice, especially for everyday goods such as groceries, medicines and school supplies. These are necessities, and no one should have to argue to pay a fair price for them. Bargaining can remain for items where prices naturally vary, such as handicrafts, second-hand goods or bulk purchases, as long as sellers are honest.

In conclusion, bargaining is an enjoyable tradition, but fairness matters more. Fixed prices protect ordinary customers and build trust, while a little room for friendly negotiation can keep the spirit of the bazaar alive.

prompt: "Co-curricular activities, such as debating, sport and drama, are as important as academic studies."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains what co-curricular activities develop: confidence, teamwork, leadership, communication, health
Explains the case for academic priority: admissions, careers and examinations depend on marks
Shows how the two can support each other, for example debating improving essays
Considers time limits and the need for balance
Concludes clearly
model:
In many colleges, the debating society, the drama club and the sports team are treated as extras, enjoyable but not serious. Marks, after all, decide admissions. Yet employers and universities increasingly ask what else a student has done. I agree that co-curricular activities are as important as academic studies, because they develop qualities that classrooms often cannot.

Debating teaches students to think quickly, organise arguments and speak confidently in front of others. Drama builds imagination, teamwork and the ability to understand different points of view. Sport develops discipline, fitness and the ability to win and lose gracefully. Leading a society or organising an event teaches planning and responsibility. These are exactly the skills that people need in interviews, at university and in the workplace.

Co-curricular activities also support wellbeing. Students under examination pressure need ways to relax, make friends and feel that they belong. A student who plays hockey after classes often returns to study with a fresher mind.

Those who disagree make a strong practical point. Admission to medical and engineering programmes depends mainly on marks and entry tests, and a trophy for debating will not replace a low score. Parents who have sacrificed to pay fees understandably want their children to focus on what will be assessed. Time is limited, and a student who spends every evening at rehearsals may fall behind.

However, the two areas are not truly in competition. A student who debates learns to structure arguments, which improves essay writing. A member of a science society may understand physics better by building projects. Many of the students who succeed in activities are also strong academically, because they have learnt to manage their time.

Balance is the key. Activities should be scheduled sensibly, and students should reduce them close to major examinations. Colleges should give them proper support, with teachers, space and recognition, rather than treating them as a waste of time.

In conclusion, co-curricular activities deserve equal importance with academic studies because they shape the whole person. Marks may open the first door, but confidence, communication and character help students walk through it and succeed on the other side.

prompt: Should children under the age of thirteen be kept off social media?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words answering this question. Present arguments on both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains the risks for young children: harmful content, contact with strangers, cyberbullying, addiction, sleep loss
Recognises the arguments for access: staying in touch, learning, digital skills, peer pressure
Discusses who is responsible: parents, platforms, schools
Suggests practical alternatives, such as supervised use or child-friendly apps
Concludes consistently
model:
It is now common to see primary school children with their own social media accounts, posting videos and chatting with people they have never met. Many platforms set a minimum age of thirteen, but it is easily ignored. I believe children under thirteen should be kept off open social media, while being allowed supervised and limited use of safer alternatives.

The risks for young children are serious. Social media contains violent, frightening and inappropriate content that children are not ready to understand. Strangers can contact them, and young children may not recognise when someone is trying to deceive them. Cyberbullying can be cruel and constant, following a child home from school. Many apps are designed to keep users scrolling, and children find it especially hard to stop, which affects their sleep, homework and outdoor play.

Children are also still forming their sense of who they are. Counting likes and comparing themselves with others can damage their confidence at a very sensitive age.

On the other hand, some argue that social media helps children stay in touch with relatives, learn new skills and become comfortable with technology they will need later. They point out that if all their classmates are online, a child who is not may feel left out. Banning access completely may also make children curious and secretive, using accounts without their parents' knowledge.

These points show that a simple ban is not enough. Parents play the most important role. They can delay giving children their own phones, keep devices in shared rooms, and talk openly about the dangers online. Children can video call grandparents with a parent nearby and use apps designed for their age, with stronger privacy settings and no contact from strangers. Schools can teach online safety, and platforms should check ages more seriously.

In conclusion, children under thirteen should be kept off open social media because the risks outweigh the benefits at that age. However, they should not be cut off from technology altogether. Guided, limited and safe use will prepare them to use social media wisely when they are older.

prompt: Should big cities ban private cars from their central areas on certain days of the week?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Consider both sides and support your view with reasons and examples.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains benefits: cleaner air, less noise, safer streets for walkers and cyclists, encouraging public transport
Explains objections: inconvenience, harm to some businesses, people with disabilities or emergencies, weak public transport
Discusses conditions needed for success, such as alternative transport and exemptions
Uses examples of city life in Pakistan
Concludes clearly
model:
Anyone who has tried to cross a busy road in the centre of a big city knows the noise, smoke and danger of heavy traffic. Some cities around the world close their central streets to private cars on certain days. Should our cities do the same? I believe they should, but only after making sure that people have other ways to travel.

The benefits are clear. Fewer cars mean less smoke and dust, which matters greatly in cities that suffer from smog. Streets become quieter and safer, so families can walk, children can cycle and elderly people can cross roads without fear. Car-free days can also show people that it is possible to live without driving everywhere, encouraging them to use buses, rickshaws or their own feet more often.

Such days can also bring life to city centres. Without traffic, streets can host markets, book fairs, food stalls and cultural events, attracting visitors and helping local businesses.

However, there are serious objections. Many people depend on their cars to reach work, especially where public transport is limited or unsafe. Shopkeepers may fear losing customers who usually drive to their shops. Elderly people, people with disabilities and those carrying heavy goods may find it hard to manage without a vehicle. Ambulances and fire engines must always be able to pass.

These objections are reasons to plan carefully, not reasons to give up. A ban should begin with one day a week, perhaps a Sunday, and a limited area. Extra buses and shuttle services should run on that day, with parking available at the edge of the zone. Emergency vehicles, delivery vans at fixed hours and people with disabilities should be exempt. Businesses should be consulted so that the change brings them customers rather than losing them.

If the experiment succeeds, it can be extended. If problems appear, they can be corrected before the scheme grows.

In conclusion, banning private cars from city centres on certain days is a good idea that could make our cities cleaner, safer and more pleasant. It will work only if it is introduced gradually, with reliable alternatives and fair exemptions.

prompt: Some students believe studying abroad offers the best education. Others think studying in their own country is the wiser choice.
task: Discuss both views and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the benefits of studying abroad: exposure, independence, different teaching methods, international networks
Explains the benefits of studying at home: lower cost, family support, local job networks, familiar culture
Mentions the challenges of studying abroad, such as cost, homesickness and adjusting to a new culture
Gives a clear personal opinion, which may depend on the student or the field
Mentions the brain-drain question or returning home with skills
Concludes clearly
model:
For many ambitious students, a place at a foreign university seems like the ultimate achievement. Others choose to study close to home and do just as well. Each path has its supporters. In my opinion, studying at home is the wiser choice for most undergraduates, while studying abroad is most valuable at a later stage or for specific fields.

Those who favour studying abroad point to wider exposure. Students meet classmates from many countries, learn different ways of thinking and become more independent as they manage their own lives. Some universities abroad have excellent laboratories and research facilities. A foreign degree may also open doors to international careers and networks.

Those who prefer studying at home make strong points too. The cost is far lower: foreign tuition fees, travel and living expenses can be very high for most Pakistani families, even with part-time work. Students at home can stay close to their families, who provide emotional and practical support during difficult years. They also build networks with local employers and professionals, which matter for finding jobs in their own country. Many Pakistani universities now offer good programmes, and their graduates succeed at home and abroad.

Studying abroad also brings challenges. Students may feel lonely and homesick, struggle with a new culture, language or climate, and find it hard to balance study with work. Some never return, and their country loses the skills it needs.

For these reasons, I believe most students should complete their first degree at home, where they can build a strong foundation at a reasonable cost and with family support. Studying abroad is often more useful later, for a master's degree or doctorate, when students are more mature, know exactly what they want to study and are more likely to receive scholarships. At that stage, they can bring back advanced skills and international experience.

Of course, there are exceptions. A student who wins a full scholarship to a strong university abroad would be wise to accept it.

In conclusion, both paths can lead to success. Studying at home is usually the more sensible first step, while studying abroad is a valuable opportunity at the right time and for the right reasons.

prompt: "Colleges should give as much attention to students' mental health as they do to their marks."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains the pressures students face: examinations, entry tests, family expectations, comparison
Explains how poor mental health affects learning, behaviour and safety
Considers objections: cost, stigma, lack of trained staff, focus on results
Suggests practical steps, such as counsellors, trained teachers, peer support, reasonable workloads
Concludes clearly and sensitively
model:
For many intermediate students, life revolves around marks. Board examinations, entry tests and family expectations create pressure that can feel overwhelming. Colleges measure marks carefully, but they rarely ask how students are actually feeling. I agree that mental health deserves as much attention as academic results.

The pressures on young people are real. Students may study for long hours with little sleep, worry constantly about admissions and compare themselves with classmates who seem to do better. Some face problems at home, financial worries or loneliness. When stress becomes too heavy, it can lead to anxiety, sadness and a loss of interest in everything, including studies.

Mental health and marks are closely connected. A student who is anxious or exhausted cannot concentrate, remember or perform well in examinations. In this sense, caring for mental health is not a distraction from academic success but one of its foundations. A calm and confident student usually learns better than a frightened one.

Some argue that colleges are places for teaching, not counselling, and that mental health is a family matter. Others worry about cost and about the stigma that still surrounds mental health in our society, which may stop students from seeking help. These concerns are understandable, but they are reasons to act carefully, not to ignore the problem.

Colleges can take practical steps. They can appoint at least one trained counsellor, or arrange visits from one, so that students have someone to talk to in confidence. Teachers can be trained to notice signs that a student is struggling and to respond with kindness rather than scolding. Assemblies and workshops can teach simple ways to manage stress, such as planning study time, sleeping properly and taking exercise. Colleges can also avoid piling tests on the same week and celebrate effort and improvement, not only top positions.

Parents have a role too. When colleges speak openly about mental health, families may feel more comfortable doing the same.

In conclusion, colleges that care only about marks ignore half of what makes students succeed. By giving mental health equal attention, they would help young people not only to pass examinations but also to grow into healthy, resilient adults.

prompt: "In business, honesty is always the best policy."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Explains how honesty builds trust, repeat customers and reputation
Recognises that dishonest traders sometimes make quick profits
Explains the long-term costs of dishonesty, such as lost customers, legal trouble and harm to others
Uses everyday examples, such as shopkeepers, online sellers or contractors
Concludes with a clear judgement
model:
Every market has two kinds of shopkeepers. One mixes old stock with new, hides defects and adjusts the scales. The other tells customers honestly what an item is worth and what is wrong with it. Who does better in the end? I agree strongly that honesty is the best policy in business, even though it does not always seem so in the short term.

The greatest asset of any business is trust. A customer who has been treated honestly returns again and again, and recommends the shop to friends and relatives. In our society, where word of mouth is powerful, a reputation for honesty can be worth more than any advertisement. A mechanic who tells a customer that a repair is not needed may lose a small fee today, but he gains a loyal customer for years.

It is true that dishonest traders sometimes make quick profits. A seller who passes off a fake product as genuine may earn more on that sale. An online shop that posts misleading pictures may attract many buyers at first. This is why some people believe that honesty is for the foolish.

However, such success rarely lasts. Cheated customers do not return, and today they can share their complaints with thousands of people through reviews and social media. A single angry post can destroy a reputation that took years to build. Dishonest businesses may also face fines, legal cases and the loss of licences.

Dishonesty also harms others in ways that go beyond money. Adulterated food or fake medicines can damage people's health. Poor-quality building materials can lead to unsafe homes. A business that cheats in such ways causes real suffering, which no profit can justify.

Honesty also brings peace of mind. An honest trader does not need to remember which lie he told to which customer, and he can face his community with dignity. Our religious and moral traditions have always praised the honest merchant for this reason.

In conclusion, honesty may sometimes mean a smaller profit today, but it builds trust, reputation and a lasting business. In the long run, it is not only the right policy but also the wisest one.

prompt: "Every student, whatever career they plan to follow, should study some science and mathematics until the end of intermediate."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains the value of basic science and mathematics in daily life: health, money, technology, evaluating claims
Explains the value of scientific thinking: evidence, reasoning, problem-solving
Recognises objections: students' different interests, heavy workloads, need for specialisation
Suggests what form this study could take, such as a general science and numeracy course
Concludes clearly
model:
In Pakistan, students usually choose their stream early: science, arts, commerce or computing. A student who chooses humanities may stop studying science and mathematics at the end of matric. I agree that every student should continue some study of science and mathematics until the end of intermediate, though not necessarily at the same level as science students.

Basic science and mathematics are part of everyday life. Understanding how diseases spread, how medicines work and why a balanced diet matters helps people make better decisions about their health. Mathematics helps with budgets, loans, discounts and understanding interest rates, all of which matter for anyone who earns or spends money. Technology now shapes every career, and a basic understanding of how it works helps people use it confidently.

Science also teaches a way of thinking. It asks for evidence, tests ideas and changes its conclusions when new facts appear. These habits protect people from rumours, fake cures and misleading advertisements. A lawyer, journalist or businessperson who can judge evidence and reason clearly will do their work better.

Those who disagree argue that students have different talents and interests. A student who loves literature or history may find advanced physics or calculus frustrating and pointless. Intermediate workloads are already heavy, and adding more subjects could lower performance in the subjects students actually need for their careers. Specialisation, they say, allows students to go deeper into what matters to them.

These are fair points, which is why the science and mathematics taught to non-science students should be different. A general course could cover practical topics: basic statistics, everyday finance, health and the human body, energy and the environment, and how scientific discoveries are made. Such a course would not require complex formulas or heavy practical work, but it would keep every student scientifically and numerically literate.

Equally, science students would benefit from some study of language, history and ethics. A balanced education helps everyone.

In conclusion, every student should keep studying some science and mathematics until the end of intermediate, in a form suited to their stream. In a world shaped by science and numbers, these subjects are not a luxury for some but a basic need for all.

prompt: "Children who grow up in villages are healthier and happier than children who grow up in cities."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains possible advantages of village childhoods: open space, fresh food, outdoor play, close communities
Explains disadvantages of village life for children: fewer hospitals, weaker schools, limited opportunities
Explains city advantages and disadvantages: facilities versus pollution, traffic, screens, small homes
Avoids sweeping generalisations and recognises variety within villages and cities
Concludes with a balanced but definite judgement
model:
Many grandparents remember childhoods spent climbing trees, swimming in canals and running across fields until sunset. Compared with city children who spend their days indoors with screens, village children seem freer and healthier. I agree only partly: village life offers real advantages, but it also has disadvantages that affect children's health and happiness.

Village childhoods have obvious strengths. Children have open space to play, cleaner air in most seasons and plenty of physical activity. Many families eat fresh vegetables, milk and grains from their own land. Communities are close, so children grow up knowing their neighbours and feeling safe among people who care for them. These conditions can help children grow strong and confident.

However, village life is not always healthy. Many villages lack nearby hospitals, specialist doctors and emergency care, so a simple illness can become serious before treatment is found. Clean drinking water and proper sanitation are not available everywhere. Schools in some rural areas are poorly equipped or short of teachers, which affects children's future opportunities and, in time, their happiness.

City children face different problems. Air pollution, heavy traffic and small homes with no gardens limit outdoor play. Many city children spend long hours on phones and tablets, eat more fast food and get little exercise. On the other hand, cities provide better hospitals, more schools and colleges, libraries, sports clubs and a wider range of activities. A city child with a park nearby and active parents can be very healthy and happy.

The truth is that conditions vary greatly. A well-off village family with a clean home and educated parents may give a child an excellent upbringing, while a poor family in a crowded city may struggle. The reverse is also true. Health and happiness depend more on a family's income, care and choices than on location alone.

In conclusion, village children often enjoy more outdoor freedom and fresh food, while city children enjoy better services and opportunities. Neither group is automatically healthier or happier. The aim should be to bring better health care and schools to villages, and more open space and outdoor activity to cities.

prompt: "Watching foreign dramas and films weakens our own culture."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Explains concerns: changing values, language, dress or lifestyle, less interest in local productions
Explains benefits: learning about other cultures, language skills, higher creative standards, tolerance
Recognises that cultures have always exchanged ideas and remain strong when confident
Discusses the role of strong local content and thoughtful viewing
Concludes clearly
model:
Young Pakistanis today can watch dramas from Turkey, films from Hollywood and series from Korea with a few taps on a phone. Some elders worry that this flood of foreign entertainment is changing how young people dress, speak and think. I agree only to a small extent: foreign dramas can influence our culture, but they need not weaken it.

The concerns are understandable. Entertainment shapes ideas about what is normal or desirable. When young people watch many foreign programmes, they may adopt fashions, slang or attitudes that differ from local values. Some may lose interest in local stories, music and languages, viewing them as old-fashioned. If local productions lose viewers, they also lose money, and fewer local stories are told.

However, there are clear benefits too. Foreign dramas and films show viewers how people in other countries live, think and solve problems. This can build understanding and tolerance. Many young people improve their English or learn other languages through films. Exposure to high-quality productions can also push local writers and directors to raise their own standards.

It is also worth remembering that cultures have always borrowed from one another. Our food, clothes, music and language already contain influences from many regions and periods of history. Culture is not a fragile glass object that breaks when it touches something new; it is a living tradition that grows. What weakens a culture is not contact with others but a loss of confidence in itself.

In fact, local dramas have proved that they can compete. Pakistani dramas have long been popular with audiences in neighbouring countries and among overseas communities, showing that strong local stories travel well.

The answer, then, is balance and confidence. Families can watch and discuss programmes together, thinking about which values to accept and which to question. Local producers can tell fresh, honest stories about our own lives. Schools can encourage interest in local literature, poetry and heritage.

In conclusion, foreign dramas and films do influence young people, but they weaken our culture only if we stop valuing and creating our own. A confident culture can enjoy the world's stories while continuing to tell its own.

prompt: "Schools and colleges should teach students how to manage money."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains why money skills matter: budgeting, saving, avoiding debt and scams, understanding loans and interest
Notes that many families may not teach these skills, or may not have them
Considers objections: crowded timetables, money being a family matter, lack of trained teachers
Suggests what such lessons could include and how they could fit the curriculum
Concludes clearly
model:
Many young people leave college able to solve complex equations but unsure how to make a monthly budget, compare two mobile packages or recognise a financial scam. Money affects every adult's life, yet it is rarely taught in classrooms. I agree that schools and colleges should teach students how to manage money.

Money skills are needed by everyone. Whether a student becomes a doctor, a shopkeeper or a teacher, they will need to plan their spending, save for the future and decide whether to borrow. Without these skills, people fall into debt, waste their income or are tricked by schemes promising quick profits. Online fraud, fake investment offers and hidden charges on loans are common, and young people are often the targets.

Not every family can teach these lessons. Some parents are excellent money managers, but others never had the chance to learn, and some families find it uncomfortable to talk about money. School lessons would give every student the same basic knowledge, regardless of background.

Some people argue that money is a private family matter and that schools should focus on academic subjects. Timetables are already crowded, and few teachers have been trained to teach finance. These are fair points, but money management does not need a whole new subject. It can be included in existing ones. Mathematics lessons can use real examples such as discounts, profit and loss, simple interest and instalments. Social studies can discuss saving, taxes and responsible spending. Islamic Studies and ethics lessons can discuss honest dealing and avoiding unnecessary debt. A few workshops a year, perhaps led by bank officers or local business owners, could cover practical topics such as opening an account and using digital payments safely.

Simple activities would make lessons memorable. Students could plan a family budget for a month, compare prices of the same item in different shops, or run a small stall at a college fair.

In conclusion, teaching money management would prepare students for real life in a way that many subjects do not. It need not be complicated or expensive, and its benefits would last for a lifetime.

prompt: "Private tuition academies do students more harm than good."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Recognises benefits: extra practice, test preparation, filling gaps left by weak teaching
Explains harms: cost to families, exhaustion, reliance on spoon-feeding, neglect of college classes
Discusses fairness for students who cannot afford academies
Suggests what colleges, families or students could do differently
Concludes with a balanced but definite judgement
model:
In most Pakistani cities, the streets near colleges are lined with banners for tuition academies promising top marks and guaranteed admissions. Many students attend college in the morning and an academy every evening. Some people believe these academies are essential; others say they harm education. I agree only partly that academies do more harm than good.

Academies do offer real benefits. Where college teaching is weak or classes are too large for questions, an academy can fill the gaps. Experienced tutors know the examination pattern well, provide practice tests and help students prepare for entry tests. For a student who has fallen behind, extra lessons in a smaller group can rebuild confidence.

However, the harms are significant. Academy fees are a heavy burden for many families, who may cut other spending to pay them. Students who study at college all day and at an academy all evening have little time left for rest, exercise or independent revision. Many become exhausted, and their health and concentration suffer.

Academies also encourage dependence. Some focus on short notes, guessed questions and memorised answers, so students learn to rely on being given material rather than working things out for themselves. This habit becomes a problem at university, where independent study is essential. In some places, students even skip college lectures because they expect to learn everything at the academy, which weakens colleges further.

There is also a question of fairness. Students whose families cannot afford academies may feel they are competing at a disadvantage, and in many cases they are.

The real issue is that academies exist largely because many colleges do not meet students' needs. The solution is to improve college teaching, with smaller classes, regular tests, and teachers who are available for questions. Families should consider whether an academy is truly needed for every subject, and students should use academies for practice and guidance rather than as a replacement for their own effort.

In conclusion, academies are neither wholly good nor wholly harmful. They help many students but also cost families dearly and encourage spoon-feeding. Their harm will shrink only when colleges become strong enough that academies are a choice rather than a necessity.

prompt: "Modern technology, which was meant to make life easier, has actually made people busier."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Gives examples of technology saving time and effort, such as washing machines, online banking, maps
Explains how technology can make people busier: constant messages, work at home, higher expectations, distraction
Considers whether the problem is technology itself or how it is used
Suggests ways to use technology so that it saves time
Concludes with a clear judgement
model:
Our grandparents washed clothes by hand, wrote letters that took weeks to arrive and queued for hours to pay bills. Today machines and apps do these jobs in minutes. Yet many people say they have less free time than ever. I largely agree that technology has made people busier, although the fault lies mainly in how we use it.

There is no doubt that technology saves effort. Washing machines, microwaves and water pumps have reduced household work. Online banking and mobile wallets have ended many queues. Maps on phones help drivers avoid traffic, and video calls save long journeys. In these ways, technology has given people time and energy they never had before.

However, much of this saved time is quickly filled. Phones bring a constant stream of messages, notifications and calls. Office workers who once left their work at the office now receive emails and group messages late at night and at weekends. Students are expected to reply instantly to class groups. Because communication is easy, people expect quick responses, and this expectation creates pressure.

Technology also raises the amount we try to do. Since tasks are faster, employers expect more of them in a day. Since information is endless, we feel we must keep up with news, videos and social media posts. Hours can vanish while scrolling, leaving people feeling busy without having achieved much.

Some argue that technology is only a tool and that people choose how to use it. This is true, and it is why the problem can be solved. People can switch off notifications, set times for checking messages, and keep phones away during meals and study. Offices can agree that staff need not reply after working hours. Families can set aside screen-free time each day.

Used in this way, technology can deliver its original promise. A student who uses an app to plan revision and then switches off the phone will find study easier, not harder.

In conclusion, technology has made many people busier because it allows constant connection and ever higher expectations. But the same tools that fill our days can free them, if we learn to control technology rather than letting it control us.

prompt: Some young people want to start their own businesses. Others prefer the security of a government job.
task: Discuss both choices and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the attraction of a government job: security, pension, fixed hours, social respect
Explains the attraction of business: independence, creativity, unlimited earning potential, creating jobs for others
Notes the risks and drawbacks of each, such as slow promotion or business failure
Gives a clear personal opinion with reasons
Considers personality, resources and timing
Concludes clearly
model:
For generations, many Pakistani parents have dreamt of their children securing a government job. Today, more young people talk about starting their own businesses, from online stores to small restaurants. Each choice has strong attractions. In my opinion, young people with suitable skills and some support should consider starting a business, though a government job remains a sensible choice for many.

A government job offers security. Salaries arrive every month, jobs are rarely lost, and there are benefits such as a pension and medical facilities. Working hours are usually fixed, leaving time for family. Such jobs are also respected in society, and parents feel reassured when their children have one.

However, government jobs also have drawbacks. Competition for them is intense, and many candidates wait years and sit many tests before getting one. Promotion can be slow, salaries may grow only modestly, and some people feel their creativity is not used.

Starting a business offers independence. Entrepreneurs make their own decisions, follow their own ideas and can earn far more if their business succeeds. They also create jobs for others, which helps the economy. With the internet, it is easier than ever to start small: selling handmade goods, offering design services or running a delivery business requires little money at first.

But business is risky. Many new businesses fail, and the owner may lose savings or borrowed money. Income can be uncertain, especially in the early years, and the work often takes long hours with no fixed holidays. Not everyone has the temperament for such uncertainty.

The right choice depends on the person. Someone who enjoys taking risks, solving problems and dealing with customers may thrive in business. Someone who values stability or has heavy family responsibilities may be wiser to seek a secure job. Timing matters too: some people work in a job for a few years, save money and gain experience, and then start a business with lower risk.

In conclusion, neither path is better for everyone. A government job brings security, while a business brings freedom and opportunity. I believe more young people should consider business, but they should do so with careful planning, realistic expectations and, ideally, some experience first.

prompt: Should households pay for water according to how much they use, so that people waste less?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words answering this question. Consider both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains the problem of water scarcity and everyday waste, such as washing cars with hoses or leaking pipes
Explains how metering and pricing could change behaviour and fund repairs
Considers objections: water as a basic need, fairness to poor families, cost of meters, trust in billing
Suggests a fair system, such as a free or cheap basic amount with higher charges for heavy use
Concludes clearly
model:
In many neighbourhoods, it is common to see a car being washed with a running hose or water overflowing from a rooftop tank for hours. At the same time, other households wait for a water tanker or queue at a public tap. Pakistan's water supply is under pressure, and waste makes the problem worse. I believe households should pay according to their use, but in a way that protects the poor.

The main argument is that people use resources more carefully when they pay for them. In many areas, households pay a fixed charge or nothing at all, no matter how much water they use. There is little reason to fix a leaking tap or to water a garden less often. If bills depended on use, families would notice the cost of waste and change their habits.

Charging by use could also raise money to improve the system. Old pipes in many cities leak large amounts of water before it reaches homes. Revenue from metered bills could fund repairs, treatment plants and new connections.

There are serious objections. Water is a basic human need, and no family should go without it because they cannot pay. Poorer households often have large families, and a simple charge per litre could fall heavily on them. Installing meters costs money, and people may not trust that the meters and bills will be accurate. In areas where the supply is irregular, charging people more for an unreliable service would seem unfair.

These objections point towards a careful design. Each household could receive a basic amount of water, enough for drinking, cooking and washing, at a very low price or free of charge. Above that amount, prices would rise, so that heavy users, such as those filling swimming pools or washing cars daily, would pay more. Meters should be checked regularly, and bills should be clear and easy to understand. The supply should be improved alongside the new charges, so that people see what they are paying for.

In conclusion, paying for water according to use is a sensible way to reduce waste and fund better services, provided it protects basic needs and is introduced fairly and transparently.

prompt: "Top sports stars are paid far more than they deserve."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Compares sports stars' earnings with the value of professions such as nursing or teaching
Explains why stars earn so much: audiences, broadcasting, sponsors, rare talent, short careers
Considers the role of stars as role models and their charitable work
Discusses whether 'deserve' means market value or social value
Concludes clearly
model:
A famous cricketer or footballer may earn more from a single advertisement than a nurse earns in many years. Many people find this unfair, since nurses, teachers and doctors save and shape lives every day. I disagree, however, that top sports stars are paid far more than they deserve, at least in the way the market measures value.

It is easy to see why the statement is popular. Society depends on teachers, doctors, farmers and sanitation workers, yet many of them earn modest salaries. Compared with their importance, the huge sums paid to athletes for playing games can seem excessive and even wasteful.

However, sports stars are not paid by the public purse; they are paid from the money that their performances generate. Millions of fans buy tickets, watch matches on television and online, and buy products that stars advertise. Broadcasters and sponsors pay large amounts because these athletes attract huge audiences. In that sense, stars earn a share of the wealth they help to create.

Top athletes also possess rare talent, developed through years of training from childhood. For every player who reaches the national team, thousands of others train just as hard and never succeed. A professional career is also short, often ending in a player's thirties, and injuries can end it suddenly. High pay during these few years must support them for the rest of their lives.

Many stars also use their fame for good. Some build schools and hospitals, support charities, or raise money during floods and other disasters. As role models, they can inspire young people to exercise, work hard and stay disciplined.

The real question is what "deserve" means. If it means value to society, then nurses and teachers deserve far more than they receive. But that is an argument for paying them better, not for paying athletes less. Reducing a cricketer's income would not raise a teacher's salary.

In conclusion, sports stars' high earnings reflect the money and attention their talent attracts, so they are not unfairly paid in market terms. The greater injustice is that essential workers are paid too little, and that is the problem society should try to fix.

prompt: "Young people should value the advice of their elders more than the information they find online."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains what elders offer: experience, knowledge of the young person, wisdom about relationships and life choices
Explains what online information offers: up-to-date facts, wide range of views, specialist knowledge
Notes the weaknesses of each: elders may be out of date; online content may be unreliable or impersonal
Distinguishes between types of questions, such as life decisions versus technical facts
Concludes with a balanced but clear judgement, written respectfully
model:
When a young person in Pakistan faces a decision about studies, career or marriage, there are now two sources of advice: the elders of the family and the endless information online. Some say young people trust the internet too much and their elders too little. I agree with this statement for questions about life and character, though not for every kind of question.

Elders offer something no website can: experience of life and knowledge of the person asking. A grandfather who has seen many years of family life understands how decisions play out over time. A mother knows her child's strengths and weaknesses. Elders can give advice about relationships, responsibility, patience and how to deal with failure, which are matters where wisdom matters more than facts. Their advice is also given with love and a real interest in the young person's future.

Online information has its own strengths. It is up to date, covers every subject and offers specialist knowledge. A student comparing university programmes, learning a new software skill or researching a scholarship will often find more accurate details online than any relative can provide. Elders may sometimes give advice based on conditions that have changed, for example about which careers are in demand.

Both sources have weaknesses. Online information can be unreliable, and much of it is written by strangers who know nothing about the reader. Social media is full of confident voices giving poor advice. Elders, for their part, may be cautious about new paths simply because they are unfamiliar.

The wise approach is to know which source suits which question. For facts, trends and technical matters, reliable websites and experts are valuable. For decisions about values, relationships and life direction, the advice of elders should carry great weight. Often the best results come from combining both: a student can research options online and then discuss them with parents and grandparents, who can help judge what suits the family and the student's character.

In conclusion, young people should value their elders' advice highly, especially on life's important decisions. The internet is a useful library, but elders are trusted guides, and a wise young person listens to both.

prompt: "Giving money to beggars on the street does more harm than good."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position, written with respect for people in poverty
Recognises the moral and religious value of charity and the real needs of many people who beg
Explains concerns: organised begging, exploitation of children, money not reaching those in need, dependence
Discusses alternatives: giving food, supporting trusted charities, helping known families directly
Considers the role of government and community in tackling poverty
Concludes with a balanced judgement
model:
At almost every traffic signal in our big cities, someone taps on car windows asking for money: an elderly man, a woman carrying a baby, a small child. Many drivers give a few coins; others look away. Does such giving help or harm? I agree only partly that it does more harm than good. Charity is a duty, but how we give matters.

Charity has a central place in our values. Our faith and culture teach generosity towards the poor, and many people who beg are in genuine need. They may be ill, elderly, disabled or without any other means of support. For them, a little money can mean a meal that day. Turning away from every person who asks can harden our hearts.

However, there are serious concerns. In some cases, begging is organised by gangs who take most of the money and force others, including children, to beg for long hours. When children earn money at traffic signals, they may be kept away from school, which traps them in poverty for life. Giving money at signals can, without our knowing it, support this exploitation. Begging in traffic is also dangerous, especially for young children.

There is also the risk of dependence. Street giving offers immediate relief but rarely changes a person's situation, and it may discourage some from seeking other help.

The answer is not to stop giving but to give more wisely. People can offer food or water instead of cash. They can give to trusted charities, welfare organisations or local mosque committees that provide food, medical care, schooling and skills training. Helping a known family in the neighbourhood, a widow or a sick labourer, ensures that help reaches someone in real need. Paying for a child's school fees can do more lasting good than many coins at a signal.

Governments and communities also have a role, through shelters, welfare programmes and action against those who exploit beggars.

In conclusion, giving money to beggars can sometimes do harm, especially when it supports exploitation. But the spirit of charity must remain. By giving thoughtfully and through trusted channels, we can make our generosity truly help those in need.

prompt: "Genetically modified crops are the best answer to feeding a growing world population."
task: To what extent do you agree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Explains in simple terms what genetically modified crops are
Gives possible benefits: higher yields, pest resistance, drought tolerance, added nutrients
Gives concerns: safety testing, dependence on seed companies, effects on other plants and insects, farmers' costs
Mentions other solutions: reducing food waste, better irrigation and storage, improved traditional varieties
Concludes with a balanced but definite judgement
model:
As the world's population grows and the climate becomes less predictable, the question of how to feed everyone becomes more urgent. Genetically modified crops, whose genes have been changed in a laboratory to give them useful qualities, are often presented as the solution. I agree that they can help, but I disagree that they are the best or only answer.

The possible benefits are significant. Some modified crops are designed to resist insect pests, so farmers need to spray fewer chemicals. Others are being developed to tolerate drought, heat or salty soil, which matters in regions where water is scarce. Crops can also be given extra nutrients, such as vitamins, to help reduce malnutrition. Higher yields from the same land could feed more people without cutting down forests for new farms.

However, there are reasonable concerns. New crops must be tested carefully to make sure they are safe to eat and do not harm the environment, for example by affecting insects or spreading genes to wild plants. Seeds are often owned by large companies, and farmers may need to buy new seed every season, which raises costs for small farmers. If pests adapt to resistant crops, the benefits may fade over time.

Moreover, hunger is not caused only by a shortage of food. A great deal of food is wasted: grain spoils in poor storage, fruit and vegetables rot during transport, and households and restaurants throw away leftovers. Many people go hungry because they cannot afford food, not because none exists. Solving these problems could feed many more people without any new technology.

Other approaches are also valuable. Better irrigation, such as drip systems, can save water. Improved traditional crop varieties, developed through careful breeding, can increase yields. Training farmers in modern methods and giving them access to fair markets and credit can raise production too.

In conclusion, genetically modified crops can be one useful tool for feeding a growing population, provided they are tested properly and are affordable for small farmers. But the best answer combines many solutions: reducing waste, improving farming methods and tackling poverty, so that food reaches everyone who needs it.

prompt: "Tall apartment buildings are the best way to house people in our growing cities."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains benefits of high-rise housing: saving land, protecting farmland, shorter commutes, services in one place
Explains drawbacks: safety in earthquakes and fires, lifts and power cuts, lack of open space, cost
Considers cultural preferences for houses and courtyards and the needs of large families
Discusses conditions such as building standards, parks and maintenance
Concludes clearly
model:
Around many of our cities, new housing schemes spread outwards each year, swallowing farmland and forcing residents to travel long distances to work. Some planners argue that the answer is to build upwards instead, with tall apartment buildings. I agree that high-rise housing is the best option for growing cities, provided it is built safely and planned well.

The strongest argument is land. When every family wants its own house, cities spread endlessly, destroying fertile fields and orchards that feed the country. Apartment buildings house many families on a small piece of land, so cities can grow without eating into farmland. This also keeps people closer to their workplaces, schools and hospitals, reducing travel time, fuel use and traffic.

High-rise housing also makes services easier to provide. Water, electricity, gas and sewerage can be supplied more efficiently to many homes in one building than to houses spread across a wide area. Shops, schools and clinics can be placed within walking distance.

There are real drawbacks. Tall buildings must be designed to withstand earthquakes and to allow people to escape quickly in a fire. Lifts and water pumps depend on electricity, so frequent power cuts can make life on upper floors difficult. Without careful planning, apartment blocks can feel crowded, with little sunlight and no space for children to play. Many families also prefer houses with courtyards, roofs and space for relatives, which suits our culture of large and joint families.

These concerns show what good high-rise housing requires. Strict building codes must be followed and checked. Buildings need backup power for lifts and pumps, proper fire exits and regular maintenance funded by residents' associations. Developments should include parks, playgrounds and community spaces. Larger flats could be designed for bigger families.

Some argue that houses are better for family life. That may be true for those who can afford them, but most new city residents cannot, and endless spreading harms everyone.

In conclusion, tall apartment buildings are the best way to house growing urban populations, because they save land and bring people closer to services. They must, however, be safe, well maintained and designed with families in mind.

prompt: "Advertising does more harm than good."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains benefits: information about products, competition and lower prices, support for free media and sport
Explains harms: creating false needs, encouraging debt, unhealthy products, unrealistic beauty standards, targeting children
Uses everyday examples from television, billboards or social media
Discusses the role of regulation and viewers' awareness
Concludes with a clear judgement
model:
Advertisements are everywhere: on billboards along the roads, between overs in cricket matches and in almost every video on our phones. They tell us what to eat, wear and buy. Some people see advertising as useful information; others see it as manipulation. I disagree that it does more harm than good, although it certainly needs limits.

Advertising has real benefits. It tells customers about new products, services and offers they might never have known about. A new business can use advertising to reach customers and compete with established brands, which encourages lower prices and better quality. Advertising also pays for much of what we enjoy for free, including television channels, sports broadcasts and many online services. Public-service advertisements spread important messages about health, road safety and saving water.

However, the harms are also real. Many advertisements try to create needs rather than meet them, persuading people that they must buy the latest phone or fashionable clothes to be happy or respected. This can push families into spending beyond their means. Advertisements for fast food and sugary drinks encourage unhealthy habits, especially among children. Some advertisements promote unrealistic ideas of beauty, such as the message that only fair skin is attractive, which can harm young people's confidence.

Children are particularly vulnerable because they cannot easily tell the difference between information and persuasion. Advertisements placed during children's programmes or inside games can shape their desires before they are able to judge.

These harms come mainly from certain kinds of advertising, not from advertising itself. Rules can reduce them. Authorities can limit advertisements for unhealthy products during children's programmes, ban misleading claims and require clear information about prices and conditions. Companies can follow ethical codes and avoid messages that insult or exclude people.

Viewers also have a role. Families and schools can teach young people to ask simple questions: what is this advertisement trying to make me feel, and do I really need this product?

In conclusion, advertising does more good than harm overall, because it informs customers, supports competition and funds free media. Its harmful forms, however, must be controlled through sensible rules and wiser viewers.

prompt: Should students in schools and colleges be placed in separate classes according to their ability?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Present arguments on both sides and make your own position clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains benefits: teaching at the right pace, stretching able students, extra support for weaker ones
Explains drawbacks: labelling, low expectations, loss of confidence, social division, unfair testing
Considers whether students can move between groups
Suggests alternatives, such as mixed classes with grouping for some subjects
Concludes consistently
model:
In many schools, students are placed in sections such as A, B and C, and everyone knows which section holds the "bright" students. Supporters say this helps teachers; critics say it labels children for years. In my view, separating students by ability can be useful in some subjects, but only if groups are flexible and every student is expected to improve.

The case for grouping is practical. In a mixed class, a teacher must explain things slowly enough for weaker students, which may bore those who already understand, or quickly enough for the strongest, which leaves others behind. When students of similar ability are taught together, the teacher can choose a suitable pace and level. Able students can be given harder problems, while those who are struggling receive more explanation and practice.

However, the drawbacks are serious. Students placed in a lower group often feel they have been labelled as failures, and they may stop trying. Teachers, too, may expect less from them, and expectations have a strong effect on results. Placement is often based on a single test, which may not reflect a student's real ability, especially if the student was ill or nervous that day. Separating students can also divide them socially, so that friendships form only within groups.

Mixed classes have their own advantages. Weaker students can learn from stronger classmates, and strong students deepen their understanding by explaining ideas to others. Classes reflect the real world, where people of different abilities must work together.

A balanced approach would combine both. Students could be grouped by ability only in subjects such as mathematics, where skills build step by step, while remaining in mixed classes for other subjects. Groups should be reviewed regularly, so that a student who improves can move up. Teachers should set high expectations for every group and avoid labels that suggest a student's limit has been reached.

In conclusion, ability grouping can help teachers match lessons to students' needs, but rigid and permanent groups do more harm than good. Flexible grouping in certain subjects, with movement between groups and high expectations for all, offers the benefits without the damage.

prompt: "Video games are a waste of time for young people."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains the possible harms: lost study time, addiction, less exercise, sleep problems, violent or unsuitable content, spending
Explains possible benefits: problem-solving, quick thinking, teamwork, relaxation, careers in game design
Distinguishes between moderate and excessive play and between types of games
Discusses the role of parents and self-control
Concludes clearly
model:
Late at night, many teenagers can be found with headphones on and eyes fixed on a screen, battling online opponents. Parents often see video games as a waste of time that steals hours from study and sleep. I disagree that games are simply a waste of time, though I accept that too much gaming is harmful.

The harms of excessive gaming are real. Games are designed to be exciting and to keep players coming back, and some young people play for many hours a day. This leaves less time for homework, exercise, family and friends. Late-night gaming disturbs sleep, which affects concentration in class. Some games contain violent or unsuitable content, and many encourage players to spend money on items inside the game.

However, games also have benefits. Many require planning, problem-solving and quick decisions. Puzzle and strategy games exercise memory and logical thinking. Online team games teach players to communicate and cooperate to reach a shared goal. After a long day of study, a short game can help a student relax, just as a walk or a television programme might.

Games can also lead to careers. The global gaming industry employs programmers, designers, artists, writers and testers. Some young Pakistanis have begun to build careers in game development and related digital fields, and an interest in games can be the first step towards learning programming.

The key difference is between moderate and excessive play. An hour of gaming after finishing homework is very different from five hours that replace sleep. The type of game also matters: a puzzle game or a sports simulation is not the same as one filled with violence.

Parents and young people both have a role. Families can agree on time limits, keep consoles and computers in shared rooms and check age ratings. Young people can learn self-control by setting their own limits and putting studies first, especially during examinations.

In conclusion, video games are not automatically a waste of time. Played in moderation and chosen wisely, they can sharpen the mind, relax the body and even open career paths. The problem lies not in the games but in letting them take over a young person's life.

prompt: "Tourism does more harm than good to the mountain valleys of northern Pakistan."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Explains the benefits of tourism: income for local families, jobs, roads and services, cultural exchange
Explains the harms: litter, pollution, unplanned construction, pressure on water and forests, traffic jams
Mentions the effect on local culture and traditions
Suggests ways to make tourism responsible, such as waste rules, planning and visitor education
Concludes with a balanced but definite judgement
model:
Every summer, crowds of visitors drive north to escape the heat of the plains. They come for green valleys, cold rivers, lakes and snow-capped peaks. But many also leave behind litter, traffic jams and hastily built hotels. Does tourism harm these beautiful regions more than it helps them? I disagree with the statement, but only on condition that tourism is managed far better than it often is.

Tourism brings much-needed income. In mountain areas, farming is often difficult and jobs are few. Hotels, guest houses, restaurants, jeep drivers, guides and handicraft sellers all earn money from visitors, and this money supports families through the long winters. Tourism also encourages the building of roads, clinics and communication networks that benefit local people as well as visitors. Meeting people from other regions can increase understanding between communities.

However, the harms are visible. Popular spots are often littered with plastic bottles, wrappers and food waste. Rivers can be polluted by sewage from hotels without proper waste systems. Unplanned construction, sometimes close to riverbanks, spoils the landscape and can be dangerous during floods. Trees are cut for building and fuel, and large numbers of vehicles create traffic jams on narrow mountain roads. Local water supplies come under pressure during peak season.

Tourism can also affect local culture. Some residents feel that visitors do not always respect their customs, dress or privacy, and traditional ways of life can change quickly when tourism becomes the main source of income.

These problems are serious, but they can be reduced. Local governments can enforce rules on building, require hotels to manage waste properly and limit construction near rivers. Visitors can be asked to carry their rubbish back with them, and bins and recycling points can be provided. Entry fees at popular sites can fund cleaning and conservation. Tourists themselves should learn to behave responsibly, respecting both nature and local people.

In conclusion, tourism brings real benefits to the northern valleys, and stopping it would hurt the people who live there. The harms come from careless and unplanned tourism. With proper rules and responsible visitors, tourism can support local communities without destroying the beauty that attracts people in the first place.

prompt: Some people believe parents should decide which career their children follow. Others think young people should make this choice for themselves.
task: Discuss both views and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the parents' view: experience, financial support, knowledge of the child, family responsibilities
Explains the young person's view: own interests, abilities, motivation and responsibility for their life
Notes the risks of each: forced careers leading to failure or unhappiness; young people choosing without information
Gives a clear personal opinion
Suggests how families can decide together, respectfully
Concludes clearly
model:
In many Pakistani families, a child's career is discussed long before the child can spell it. Some parents plan for their son to be a doctor or their daughter to be an engineer from an early age. Others leave the choice entirely to the young person. Each view has merit. In my opinion, young people should make the final choice, but with their parents' guidance and blessing.

Parents who wish to decide have understandable reasons. They have more experience of life and of the job market. They often pay for their children's education and may have sacrificed a great deal to do so. They know their children well and want them to have a secure and respected future. In a family where a business or profession has been built over generations, parents may also hope that a child will continue it.

Those who believe young people should choose argue that a career shapes a person's whole adult life. It is the young person who will study the subject, sit the examinations and do the work every day for decades. A student forced into medicine without any interest may struggle, fail or feel unhappy for years. On the other hand, a student who chooses a field they enjoy is more likely to work hard and succeed.

Both views have risks. Parents may push children towards a few traditional professions and overlook new fields where their children could thrive, such as design, data science or media. Young people, meanwhile, may choose based on a passing interest, a friend's choice or a social media trend, without understanding what a career really involves.

The best solution is partnership. Young people should research careers, talk to people in those fields and present their reasons clearly and respectfully. Parents should listen, share their experience and point out practical concerns, without forcing a decision. Career counsellors and teachers can help both sides by giving accurate information about abilities and opportunities.

In conclusion, parents' guidance is valuable, but the final decision should belong to the young person who must live with it. When families decide together, with respect on both sides, children are more likely to choose wisely and to have their parents' support along the way.

prompt: Should college canteens be allowed to sell only healthy food?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words answering this question. Consider both sides and support your view with reasons and examples.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains the health case: rising obesity and diabetes risk, energy and concentration, setting good habits
Explains objections: student choice, cost, taste, students buying junk food outside instead
Discusses what 'healthy' food could be in a Pakistani canteen, keeping it affordable and appealing
Suggests a practical policy, such as limits on fried food and fizzy drinks rather than a total ban
Concludes clearly
model:
In many college canteens, the most popular items are samosas, pakoras, chips and fizzy drinks. They are cheap, quick and tasty, and students eat them almost every day. Some people believe canteens should be allowed to sell only healthy food. I agree that canteens should mainly offer healthy options, but a complete ban on less healthy food would be difficult and might not work.

The health case is strong. Students who eat fried snacks and sugary drinks every day are more likely to gain weight and develop health problems later in life. Heavy, oily food can also make students feel sleepy in afternoon classes, while balanced meals provide steady energy for study. Since students spend most of their day at college, the canteen strongly influences their eating habits, and habits formed at this age often last.

There are, however, fair objections. College students are young adults who should be free to make their own choices. If the canteen sells only salads and fruit, many students will simply buy samosas and soft drinks from stalls outside the gate. Healthy food can also be more expensive, and canteen owners worry about losing customers and income. If the food is not tasty or affordable, it will not be eaten.

Healthy food does not have to mean unfamiliar or expensive food. A canteen could serve daal and rice, chana chaat, chapati rolls with grilled chicken or vegetables, seasonal fruit, yoghurt, lassi and fresh juices without added sugar. Many of these dishes are already part of our diet and can be sold at reasonable prices.

A practical policy would make healthy food the main offer while limiting unhealthy items. Fried snacks could be sold only on certain days or in smaller portions, and fizzy drinks could be replaced by water and lassi. Healthy items could be priced lower than unhealthy ones. Colleges could also teach students about nutrition, so they understand why these changes matter.

In conclusion, college canteens should focus on healthy food, but through gradual changes, affordable prices and tasty choices rather than a strict ban. The aim is to help students choose well, not simply to forbid what they enjoy.

prompt: "Downloading pirated films, books and software is wrong, even if almost everyone does it."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains why piracy is wrong: taking creators' work without paying, harm to local writers, artists and developers
Recognises the reasons people pirate: high prices, lack of legal options, the belief that no one is harmed
Answers the 'everyone does it' argument directly
Mentions legal and affordable alternatives, such as libraries, free software and low-cost subscriptions
Concludes clearly
model:
For many young people, downloading a film, a textbook or a piece of software without paying is so common that it hardly seems like a decision at all. Friends share links, and websites offer anything for free. Yet I agree that piracy is wrong, even when almost everyone does it.

The basic reason is simple: a film, book or program is someone's work. Writers spend years on a novel, programmers spend months building software, and hundreds of people work on a single film. When we download their work without paying, we take something that belongs to them, just as surely as if we took a book from a shop without paying. The fact that a digital copy costs nothing to make does not change the fact that the work itself has value.

Piracy also harms our own creative industries. Pakistani musicians, film-makers, authors and software developers need income to continue their work. If their products are copied freely, they earn little, and fewer people can afford to make a living from creative work. Large foreign companies may survive piracy, but small local creators often cannot.

People give understandable reasons for piracy. Some products are expensive compared with local incomes, and some are not legally available in Pakistan at all. Many believe that no one is really harmed by one download. These concerns are real, and companies should offer fairer prices for different countries. But a high price is a reason to look for an alternative, not a reason to take something without permission.

The argument that "everyone does it" is the weakest of all. Many wrong things are common, from littering to cheating in examinations, and their popularity does not make them right. Right and wrong do not depend on how many people are watching.

Fortunately, there are legal alternatives. Libraries lend books, many universities provide software to their students, and free programs exist for almost every common task. Low-cost streaming services and digital bookstores are now widely available.

In conclusion, piracy is wrong because it takes creators' work without their permission and weakens the industries that produce it. Choosing legal options, even when piracy is easy, is a small but real act of honesty.

prompt: "Scientists should be free to research any subject they choose."
task: To what extent do you agree with this statement? Write an essay of about 300-400 words with reasons and examples.
points: Takes a clear position
Explains the value of freedom: unexpected discoveries, curiosity-driven research leading to practical benefits
Explains the need for limits: safety, ethics, harm to people or animals, dangerous technologies
Gives examples of areas where rules are needed, such as experiments on humans or dangerous microbes
Discusses who should set limits and how, such as ethics committees and laws
Concludes with a balanced but definite judgement
model:
Many of the greatest discoveries in history came from scientists who followed their curiosity, not a plan. Yet science has also produced dangerous weapons and harmful experiments. Should scientists be free to research anything they choose? I agree to a large extent, but I believe some limits are necessary to protect people and the planet.

Freedom is essential to science. Researchers often cannot predict which questions will lead to useful results. Studies that seemed purely theoretical, such as early work on electricity, light or the structure of atoms, later led to technologies that transformed daily life, from electric power to medical imaging. If governments or companies decided in advance which subjects were worth studying, many of these breakthroughs might never have happened. Free inquiry also allows scientists to question accepted ideas, which is how knowledge improves.

However, complete freedom is dangerous. Some research directly involves people, animals or the environment, and it can cause harm if it is not controlled. History contains examples of experiments carried out on people without their consent, which caused terrible suffering. Research on dangerous microbes, powerful weapons or technologies that could be misused needs strict safety rules, because an accident or misuse could affect millions.
