For this reason, most countries require research involving people to be approved by ethics committees, which check that participants give informed consent and are not put at unnecessary risk. Laboratories that handle dangerous materials must meet safety standards. These rules do not stop science; they make sure it is done responsibly.

The challenge is to set limits without stifling curiosity. Rules should focus on methods and risks, such as how an experiment is carried out and who could be harmed, rather than on banning ideas or subjects. Decisions about limits should involve not only scientists but also doctors, ethicists, lawyers and members of the public, since everyone is affected by scientific progress.

In conclusion, scientists should generally be free to choose what they study, because curiosity drives discovery. But this freedom must operate within clear ethical and safety rules. Freedom with responsibility is what allows science to benefit humanity without causing harm.

prompt: Should cities enforce strict rules to control noise from vehicles, loudspeakers and construction?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Consider both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains the harms of noise: stress, poor sleep, hearing damage, difficulty studying, harm to patients and the elderly
Identifies common sources: pressure horns, modified exhausts, loudspeakers, generators, late-night construction
Considers objections: livelihoods, celebrations and traditions, difficulty of enforcement
Suggests fair and practical rules, such as time limits, quiet zones near hospitals and schools, and fines
Concludes clearly
model:
Anyone who lives in a big city knows the sound of pressure horns, motorbikes with modified silencers, generators and construction machines working late into the night. Add loudspeakers at weddings and events, and some neighbourhoods are rarely quiet. I believe cities should enforce strict noise rules, applied fairly and sensibly.

Noise is more than an annoyance. Constant loud noise causes stress, headaches and irritability. When it continues at night, it disturbs sleep, which affects people's health and their ability to work or study the next day. Long exposure to very loud sounds can damage hearing. Students preparing for examinations, patients recovering in hospitals, babies and elderly people suffer most.

Many sources of noise could easily be controlled. Pressure horns and modified exhausts serve no real purpose except to be loud. Construction work could be limited to daytime hours. Generators could be fitted with silencers, and loudspeakers at events could be kept at reasonable levels and switched off at a fixed time.

Some people object that noise rules could hurt livelihoods. Builders need to finish work on time, and shopkeepers use loudspeakers to attract customers. Others argue that celebrations such as weddings are part of our culture and should not be restricted. They also point out that rules already exist in many places but are rarely enforced, so new rules may change nothing.

These objections deserve consideration, but they do not justify the present situation. Rules can respect livelihoods and traditions while protecting public health. Construction could be permitted during the day and restricted late at night. Celebrations could continue, with loudspeakers turned down after a reasonable hour. Quiet zones could be marked around hospitals, schools and residential areas. Traffic police could fine vehicles with pressure horns or illegal exhausts, and fines could rise for repeat offenders.

Enforcement must be consistent and fair, applying to everyone. Public awareness campaigns can also help people understand that noise harms their neighbours, and that being considerate is a shared responsibility.

In conclusion, cities should enforce strict noise rules, because noise harms health, sleep and learning. With sensible timings, quiet zones and fair enforcement, such rules can protect residents without stopping work or celebration.

prompt: "Festivals and celebrations such as Eid have become too focused on shopping and spending."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples, and writing respectfully.
points: States a clear position
Describes the true spirit of festivals: gratitude, family, charity, sharing with neighbours and the poor
Explains the pressures of spending: new clothes, gifts, competition, debt, advertising
Recognises the positive side of spending: joy for children, income for tailors, traders and workers
Suggests how families can keep the spirit while controlling spending
Concludes clearly and respectfully
model:
In the days before Eid, markets stay open late into the night, tailors are overwhelmed with orders and shoppers crowd every bazaar. Advertisements urge families to buy new clothes, shoes, sweets and gifts. Many people feel that the celebration has become more about spending than about its true meaning. I largely agree, though spending itself is not the problem.

The real spirit of Eid lies in gratitude, family and generosity. It is a time to thank God, to visit relatives, to forgive old quarrels and to share with those in need. Charity is central to the occasion, so that poorer families can also celebrate. These values do not depend on how much money anyone spends.

However, social pressure has made spending feel compulsory. Families compete to show off new outfits, expensive gifts and lavish meals. Children compare their clothes and Eidi with those of their cousins. Families with limited incomes may feel ashamed if they cannot keep up, and some even borrow money to do so. Advertising adds to the pressure, presenting the festival as a shopping season. In this atmosphere, the quieter values of the occasion can be overlooked.

At the same time, spending has a positive side. Buying new clothes for children brings them real joy, and there is nothing wrong with celebrating in comfort. Festival shopping also provides income for tailors, shopkeepers, shoemakers, bakers and many daily-wage workers, who rely on this season for a large part of their yearly earnings.

The answer lies in balance. Families can set a budget and stick to it, buying what they can afford without competing with others. Parents can teach children that the value of Eid lies in prayer, family and kindness, not in the price of their clothes. Part of the festival budget can be set aside for charity, helping a needy family celebrate too. Communities can organise shared meals, and relatives can visit one another with simple gifts.

In conclusion, festivals have become too focused on shopping for many families, mainly because of social pressure. By spending sensibly and remembering the true spirit of the occasion, we can keep celebrations joyful, generous and meaningful for everyone.

prompt: "Cash should be completely replaced by digital payments."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains benefits of digital payments: convenience, safety from theft, records, transparency, less tax evasion
Explains problems with removing cash: people without phones, internet or bank accounts; elderly users; fraud; network failures
Considers privacy and dependence on technology
Suggests a realistic path, such as encouraging digital payments while keeping cash available
Concludes clearly
model:
Paying for groceries, school fees and even a rickshaw ride with a mobile app is becoming common in Pakistan's cities. Mobile wallets and bank apps let people send money in seconds. Some believe cash should disappear altogether. I disagree: digital payments should be encouraged strongly, but cash should remain available.

Digital payments have many advantages. They are convenient, saving trips to banks and the trouble of carrying exact change. They are safer from street theft, since there is no wallet full of notes to snatch. Every transaction leaves a record, which helps families track their spending and resolve disputes. For the economy, digital payments make business more transparent, which can reduce tax evasion and corruption.

However, removing cash completely would cause serious problems. Many people, especially in rural areas, do not have bank accounts, smartphones or reliable internet. Elderly people may find apps confusing and may be more easily tricked by fraudsters. Daily-wage workers, small vendors and farmers often deal entirely in cash. Forcing them to switch suddenly could cut them off from the economy.

Digital systems also have weaknesses. Network failures, power cuts or technical faults can stop payments at the worst moments. Online fraud, such as fake calls asking for a code or links that steal account details, is a growing problem, and its victims are often those with the least experience. Some people also worry about privacy, since every digital payment can be traced.

A complete switch would also make the whole economy dependent on technology. If a major system failed, people could be left unable to buy food or medicine. Cash, though old-fashioned, works without electricity or internet.

A realistic path is to encourage digital payments while keeping cash as a backup. Governments and banks can make accounts easy to open, reduce charges and teach people, especially elderly and rural users, how to use apps safely. Businesses can offer digital options alongside cash. Over time, as access and trust grow, more people will choose digital payments willingly.

In conclusion, digital payments offer speed, safety and transparency, but cash still serves millions of people and protects the economy against failure. The goal should be choice, not compulsion, with digital payments growing naturally while cash remains available.

prompt: Should uniforms be compulsory for students in colleges?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Present arguments on both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains benefits: equality between rich and poor students, discipline, identity, security, saving time
Explains objections: young adults' freedom, cost of uniforms, comfort in hot weather, self-expression
Considers the age of college students compared with school children
Suggests a practical compromise, if that is the position, such as a simple dress code
Concludes consistently
model:
Most Pakistani students wear a uniform throughout their school years. When they reach college, some institutions continue the rule, while others allow students to wear what they like. Should uniforms be compulsory at college level? I believe they should, though the uniform should be simple, affordable and comfortable.

The strongest argument for uniforms is equality. When every student wears the same clothes, the difference between rich and poor families is less visible. Students from modest backgrounds do not feel pressure to buy expensive fashionable outfits, and no one is judged by brand names. This helps students focus on their studies and friendships rather than appearance.

Uniforms also create a sense of identity and discipline. Students feel they belong to an institution and represent it in public. Staff and security guards can quickly recognise who belongs on the campus, which improves safety. Uniforms also save time and arguments at home each morning, since there is no need to decide what to wear.

Those who oppose uniforms make reasonable points. College students are young adults, and many feel they should be trusted to dress responsibly. Clothing can be a form of self-expression, and some students feel uniforms treat them like children. Uniforms cost money, and families with several children may struggle to buy them. Heavy fabrics or blazers can be uncomfortable in hot summers.

These objections suggest how a uniform policy should be designed, rather than proving that uniforms are wrong. A college uniform could be simple, such as a plain shalwar kameez or shirt and trousers in college colours, made of light cotton suitable for the climate. It should be available at reasonable prices, and colleges could help needy students through second-hand uniform schemes. Students could be consulted when choosing the design, giving them a sense of ownership.

Some colleges choose a dress code instead, such as modest, neat clothing without logos or slogans. This is a reasonable middle path, though it is harder to enforce and does not remove differences in wealth as fully.

In conclusion, compulsory uniforms in colleges promote equality, discipline and safety. If they are simple, comfortable and affordable, they offer these benefits without placing an unfair burden on students or their families.

prompt: "Smartphones have made young people less patient."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains how instant answers, short videos and quick replies can reduce patience and attention
Gives examples, such as skipping long videos, struggling to read long texts or wanting instant replies
Considers counter-arguments: patience varies by person; phones can also teach skills that need patience
Suggests ways to rebuild patience and concentration
Concludes clearly
model:
A video that takes more than a few seconds to load is closed. A message that is not answered within minutes causes worry. A long chapter in a textbook feels impossible to finish. These everyday experiences suggest that smartphones have changed how patient young people are. I largely agree with the statement, though phones are not the only cause, and the effect can be reversed.

Smartphones offer instant results. A question typed into a search engine is answered in a second. Food, rides and shopping arrive at the touch of a button. Short videos, often less than a minute long, deliver entertainment in small, rapid bursts. When young people grow used to this speed, ordinary activities that take time, such as reading a novel, solving a difficult mathematics problem or waiting in a queue, can feel unbearably slow.

Constant notifications also train the mind to switch attention frequently. A student studying for an hour may check the phone many times, never settling into deep concentration. Over time, it becomes harder to stay with one task, and the habit of patience weakens.

However, it would be unfair to blame phones entirely or to describe all young people in the same way. Patience differs from person to person, and many teenagers who use smartphones still spend hours practising cricket, memorising long texts or learning to code. Phones can even teach patience: learning a language through an app, practising a musical instrument with online lessons or completing a long online course all require steady effort.

The key issue is how phones are used. If they are used mainly for quick entertainment, patience suffers. If they are used for learning and purposeful activities, they need not harm it.

Patience and concentration can be rebuilt. Young people can switch off notifications while studying, keep phones out of reach for set periods and gradually increase the time they spend reading or working without interruption. Activities such as sport, cooking, gardening or reading physical books also train the mind to wait and persist.

In conclusion, smartphones have made many young people less patient by offering constant speed and distraction. But patience is a skill, not a fixed quality, and with conscious effort it can be strengthened again.

prompt: "Every household should be required by law to separate its rubbish for recycling."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains the benefits of separating waste: more recycling, less landfill, cleaner streets, income from recyclables
Explains difficulties: lack of collection systems, mixing at collection, awareness, enforcement, small homes
Mentions the role of informal waste collectors and kabaris
Suggests a practical approach, such as starting with awareness and pilot areas before strict penalties
Concludes clearly
model:
Walk past an empty plot in almost any town and you may see a mixed heap of food scraps, plastic, paper and glass. Much of this waste could be recycled or composted, yet it ends up being burnt or dumped. Some people believe households should be legally required to separate their rubbish. I agree in principle, but the law must come with a proper system to support it.

Separating waste at home has clear benefits. When food waste is kept apart, it can be turned into compost for gardens and farms. Clean paper, plastic, glass and metal can be recycled, saving raw materials and energy. Less waste goes to dumps, which reduces bad smells, flies and the smoke from burning rubbish. Streets and drains stay cleaner, reducing flooding in the monsoon.

Pakistan already has an informal recycling system. Kabaris buy old newspapers, bottles and metal from households, and waste pickers collect recyclable items from bins and dumps. Separating waste at home would make their work safer and more productive, and give them a better income.

However, a law on its own would face difficulties. In many areas, there is no separate collection: even if families sort their rubbish, the collection vehicle may mix it all together again, which quickly discourages people. Many households are not aware of what can be recycled. Small homes may lack space for several bins. Checking every household and fining those who do not comply would be very difficult.

For these reasons, the law should be introduced step by step. Municipal authorities should first provide separate collection for at least two types of waste, such as wet waste and dry waste. Awareness campaigns in schools, mosques and media can explain why separating matters and how to do it. Pilot projects in a few neighbourhoods can show success before the system spreads. Once collection is reliable, penalties for those who refuse to separate their waste would be fair.

In conclusion, requiring households to separate rubbish is a good idea that would reduce pollution and support recycling. But it will work only if authorities first build the collection system and help people understand their role.

prompt: Some people believe it is better to be excellent at one thing. Others think it is better to be good at many different things.
task: Discuss both views and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the case for specialisation: expertise, professional demand, depth, higher earnings
Explains the case for broad skills: adaptability, creativity, more career options, coping with change
Uses examples from studies, careers or sport
Gives a clear personal opinion
Considers combining depth and breadth
Concludes clearly
model:
A surgeon who has performed one kind of operation thousands of times and a manager who can handle finance, people and technology both earn respect. One is a specialist; the other has broad skills. Which is better? In my opinion, the best approach is to become excellent at one main thing while remaining reasonably good at several others.

Supporters of specialisation argue that the modern world rewards expertise. Complex fields such as medicine, engineering and law require years of focused study, and people want the best specialist when their health or money is at stake. Specialists can often command higher salaries because their skills are rare. Excellence in one area also brings confidence and recognition; a famous fast bowler is remembered for his bowling, not for being an average batsman too.

Supporters of broad skills argue that the world is changing quickly. Jobs that exist today may disappear, and new ones may appear. A person with several skills can adapt more easily, moving from one role to another. Broad knowledge also encourages creativity, since new ideas often come from combining different fields, such as using computing in agriculture or design in medicine. Many employers also look for people who can communicate, manage projects and solve problems in addition to technical knowledge.

Both approaches have risks. A narrow specialist may struggle if their field declines or changes. A person who knows a little about everything may never develop the depth needed to stand out or be trusted with difficult tasks.

For this reason, I believe young people should aim for a combination. They should choose one area, such as a subject or profession, and work hard to become truly excellent at it. At the same time, they should develop supporting skills: clear writing and speaking, basic computer skills, managing money and working in teams. A doctor who can also communicate well and use technology confidently, for example, is more valuable than one who has only medical knowledge.

In conclusion, both specialisation and broad skills have value. The strongest position is to have depth in one field and breadth around it, so that a person is both an expert and adaptable to change.

prompt: Should villages receive the same facilities as cities, such as hospitals, colleges and fast internet, even if this costs more per person?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words answering this question. Consider both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains fairness and the rights of rural citizens to health, education and connection
Explains practical benefits: less migration to cities, local development, better farming
Recognises the higher cost per person and limited budgets
Suggests efficient solutions, such as shared facilities for groups of villages, mobile clinics or online services
Concludes clearly
model:
A pregnant woman in a remote village may have to travel for hours on a rough road to reach a hospital. A bright student may give up on college because the nearest one is in a distant city. Meanwhile, city residents enjoy hospitals, universities and fast internet close at hand. Should villages receive the same facilities, even if it costs more per person? I believe they should receive equal access to essential services, though not always in the same form.

The first argument is fairness. Villagers are citizens with the same rights as city dwellers. Health care, education and communication are basic needs, not luxuries. A child born in a village should not have fewer chances in life simply because of where he or she was born.

There are also practical benefits. When villages lack facilities, people move to cities in large numbers, which crowds urban areas and leaves rural areas without young, educated people. Good facilities in villages would allow families to stay, and educated people could work locally as teachers, doctors and business owners. Fast internet would allow farmers to check prices and weather forecasts and allow young people to study online or work as freelancers.

On the other hand, providing services to scattered villages costs more per person. Building a hospital for a few thousand people is expensive, and keeping doctors and teachers in remote areas is difficult. Government budgets are limited, and money spent in one place cannot be spent in another.

These challenges call for smart solutions rather than neglect. Instead of a full hospital in every village, a well-equipped health centre could serve a cluster of villages, with ambulances to reach bigger hospitals. Mobile clinics and doctors available through video consultations can bring specialist advice to remote areas. Colleges could open campuses in district towns, with transport for nearby villages. Expanding internet coverage, often cheaper than building new buildings, could connect rural people to online education, banking and health services.

In conclusion, villages should receive equal access to essential facilities, even if the cost per person is higher. With careful planning and modern technology, fairness can be achieved without wasting money.

prompt: "In the days before an examination, a good night's sleep matters more than extra hours of study."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains how sleep helps memory, concentration and calm under pressure
Explains the effects of sleeplessness: tiredness, careless mistakes, anxiety, illness
Recognises the need for steady preparation earlier, so that sleep is possible
Gives practical advice for the days before an examination
Concludes clearly
model:
In the days before board examinations, many students stay awake until dawn, surrounded by notes and cups of tea. They believe every extra hour of study will add marks. Yet many of them walk into the examination hall exhausted and forget answers they knew well. I agree that, just before an examination, sleep matters more than extra study.

Sleep is not wasted time. During sleep, the brain organises and stores what we have learnt during the day, helping us remember it later. A student who studies a topic in the evening and then sleeps well is more likely to recall it the next morning than one who stays awake revising it all night. Sleep also restores concentration, so that a rested student reads questions carefully and thinks clearly.

Lack of sleep has the opposite effect. A tired student makes careless mistakes, misreads questions and struggles to complete long answers in time. Exhaustion increases anxiety, so small difficulties seem overwhelming. Students who repeatedly skip sleep may even fall ill during the examination period, losing far more than a few hours of revision.

It is true that study cannot be neglected. A student who has not prepared during the year cannot rely on sleep alone to pass. But this is exactly the point: preparation should be spread over weeks and months, so that the final days are used for light revision rather than desperate cramming. Students who plan their studies well can afford to sleep properly before an examination.

Some argue that a few late nights are unavoidable, especially when syllabuses are long. Occasional late nights earlier in the year may be manageable, but the night before an examination is the worst time to lose sleep, because the student needs a fresh mind the next day.

In the final days, students should revise key points, practise a few past questions and stop studying at a reasonable hour. Avoiding screens late at night, eating lightly and going to bed at a regular time will improve the quality of sleep.

In conclusion, sleep is one of the most powerful tools for examination success. Extra hours of study cannot replace a clear, rested mind, so students should treat sleep as part of their preparation, not an enemy of it.

prompt: "In the age of instant messages, handwritten letters and cards still have an important place."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains what handwritten messages offer: effort, personal touch, keepsakes, emotional value
Explains why instant messages dominate: speed, low cost, convenience, reaching people far away
Gives examples of occasions where handwritten notes matter, such as Eid cards, thank-you notes or letters to elders
Mentions benefits for handwriting and thoughtful expression
Concludes clearly
model:
Many families still keep a box of old letters and Eid cards from grandparents, aunts and friends. The faded ink and familiar handwriting bring back memories that a phone message rarely does. Today, almost all communication happens through instant messages. Do handwritten letters and cards still matter? I agree that they do, though for special occasions rather than everyday contact.

Instant messages have clear advantages. They arrive in seconds, cost almost nothing and can include photographs, voice notes and videos. They allow families separated by long distances to stay in daily contact. For quick questions, news and arrangements, no one would choose to write a letter.

However, handwritten messages offer something that instant messages cannot. They show effort. Choosing a card, thinking carefully about the words and writing them by hand takes time, and the receiver knows it. This makes the message feel more personal and sincere. A handwritten thank-you note to a teacher or a letter to a grandparent can mean far more than a quick text.

Handwritten letters also last. Phone messages are easily lost among hundreds of others, deleted or forgotten when a phone is changed. A letter or card can be kept for years, reread and even passed down to children. Such keepsakes become part of family history.

Writing by hand also benefits the writer. It encourages slower, more careful thought, so people often express themselves more fully. It also keeps handwriting skills alive, which students still need in examinations.

There are occasions when handwritten messages are especially valuable: Eid and wedding cards, notes of thanks or apology, letters to elderly relatives who may not use smartphones, and messages to friends on important days. In these moments, a few handwritten lines can strengthen relationships in a lasting way.

Some argue that handwritten messages are old-fashioned and wasteful of paper and time. Yet their rarity is exactly what makes them special today.

In conclusion, instant messages are ideal for everyday communication, but handwritten letters and cards still have an important place. Used for meaningful occasions, they carry a warmth and permanence that digital messages cannot match.

prompt: "Being kind is more important than being right."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples from daily life.
points: States a clear position
Explains what the statement means in everyday disagreements and arguments
Explains the value of kindness: relationships, peace in families, respect, wellbeing
Explains when being right matters, such as safety, justice, honesty, facts in medicine or science
Shows how kindness and truth can be combined
Concludes with a clear judgement
model:
In a family argument about who forgot to pay a bill, or a heated debate with a friend about cricket, many of us want above all to prove that we are right. We may win the argument but hurt someone we care about. The statement suggests that kindness should come first. I agree in most everyday situations, but not when important truths are at stake.

In daily life, many disagreements are about small matters. Insisting on being right in such cases often damages relationships. A sibling who is constantly corrected may feel humiliated, and a friend who is forced to admit a mistake may become distant. Choosing kindness, perhaps by letting a small point go or admitting that both sides have a point, keeps peace in families and friendships. People remember how we made them feel long after they forget who won the argument.

Kindness also shows respect. Speaking gently, listening carefully and avoiding sarcasm make others feel valued. Most moral and religious teachings encourage gentle speech and forgiveness, recognising that harsh words can wound deeply.

However, there are situations where being right truly matters. If a friend is about to take a dangerous shortcut on a motorbike, or a relative believes a false medical claim that could harm their health, staying silent to be kind would be a mistake. In matters of safety, justice and honesty, the truth must be spoken. A teacher who never corrects mistakes is not being kind; she is failing her students.

The best approach is to combine truth with kindness. We can correct someone without mocking them, disagree without raising our voices and choose the right time and place to speak. Instead of saying, "You are completely wrong," we can say, "I see it differently. Can I explain why?" In this way, we protect both the truth and the relationship.

In conclusion, in most everyday disagreements, kindness is more important than proving ourselves right. But when the truth affects safety, fairness or wellbeing, it must be spoken, gently but clearly. True wisdom lies in knowing which situation we are in.

prompt: Should robots and machines take over dangerous jobs that are currently done by people?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Consider both sides and support your view with reasons and examples.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains dangerous jobs, such as mining, sewer cleaning, bomb disposal, firefighting or handling chemicals
Explains benefits: saving lives, fewer injuries, working in extreme conditions, accuracy
Explains concerns: job losses for poor workers, cost, maintenance, machine failure, need for human judgement
Suggests how to manage the change, such as retraining workers and using robots alongside people
Concludes clearly
model:
Every year, workers around the world are injured or killed in coal mines, sewers, factories and building sites. In Pakistan, sanitation workers who enter blocked sewers without protection face particular danger. As robots and machines become more capable, many people ask whether they should do these dangerous jobs instead. I believe they should, as long as workers are supported through the change.

The most important reason is to save lives. Machines can enter collapsed buildings, inspect sewers filled with toxic gases, defuse explosives and handle dangerous chemicals without risking human life. Robots can work in extreme heat, cold or darkness, and they do not suffer from fatigue. Even partial automation, such as machines to clear sewers or remote-controlled equipment in mines, can greatly reduce injuries.

Machines can also be more precise and consistent. In factories, robotic arms can handle heavy or sharp materials repeatedly without accidents, improving both safety and quality.

However, there are real concerns. Many dangerous jobs are done by poor workers who have few other options. If machines replace them, they may lose their only source of income. Robots are expensive to buy and maintain, and they need trained technicians and reliable electricity. Machines can also break down or fail in unexpected situations, and some tasks, such as rescuing people in a disaster, require human judgement and compassion that machines do not have.

These concerns suggest how the change should be managed. Workers whose jobs are automated should be retrained to operate, supervise and maintain the machines. Governments and employers can share the cost of equipment, starting with the most dangerous tasks, such as entering sewers or handling explosives. Robots and humans can work together: a robot might enter a dangerous area first, while a trained person controls it from a safe distance and makes the final decisions.

Some argue that improving safety equipment and training is cheaper than buying robots. This is often true and should be done immediately. But for the most dangerous tasks, removing people from harm is the only complete solution.

In conclusion, robots and machines should take over dangerous jobs wherever possible, because human lives are more valuable than any machine. The change must be fair, protecting workers' livelihoods while protecting their lives.

prompt: "Lending money to friends is the quickest way to spoil a friendship."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and everyday examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains how loans can damage friendships: late repayment, embarrassment, resentment, avoidance
Explains how helping a friend in need can strengthen a friendship
Gives everyday examples, such as small loans for fees, phones or emergencies
Suggests sensible ways to lend: clear terms, only what one can afford to lose, or giving instead of lending
Concludes clearly
model:
Almost everyone has lent money to a friend at some point, perhaps a few hundred rupees for a meal, or a larger sum for fees or an emergency. Sometimes the money is returned on time and the friendship continues. Sometimes it is never mentioned again, and the friendship quietly fades. I agree only partly that lending money spoils friendships: it can, but it does not have to.

There is no doubt that loans can cause problems. When a friend delays repayment, the lender may feel hurt and taken advantage of, but too embarrassed to ask. The borrower may feel guilty and begin to avoid the lender, skipping meetings or ignoring calls. Small misunderstandings about when the money should be returned can turn into resentment. What began as an act of kindness ends as a source of tension.

However, refusing to help a friend in real need can also damage a friendship. If a friend's father falls ill and the family needs money for treatment, standing back may feel cold and selfish. True friendship includes supporting each other in difficult times, and a loan given at such a moment can deepen trust and gratitude for many years.

The problem is usually not lending itself but the way it is done. Several simple practices can protect a friendship. First, lend only what you can afford to lose, so that a delay does not cause you hardship. Second, agree clearly on when and how the money will be repaid, even if it feels awkward. For larger amounts, writing it down is wise, as our religious teachings themselves recommend for debts. Third, if you cannot lend, say so politely and honestly rather than making excuses.

Sometimes it is better to give rather than lend. If a friend needs a small amount and you can afford it, giving it as a gift avoids any future discomfort.

Borrowers also have responsibilities. They should repay on time, or explain honestly if they cannot, rather than avoiding the lender.

In conclusion, lending money can spoil a friendship when it is done carelessly. But with clear terms, honesty on both sides and generosity where possible, it can also be a way of showing that a friendship is real.

prompt: Some people believe reading books is the best way to learn. Others think educational videos teach more effectively.
task: Compare the two views and give your own opinion in an essay of about 300-400 words.
points: Explains the strengths of books: depth, careful argument, concentration, vocabulary, reliability of edited texts
Explains the strengths of videos: visual explanation, demonstrations, engagement, easy access
Notes the weaknesses of each, such as passive watching or difficult texts for beginners
Gives a clear personal opinion, which may depend on the subject or purpose
Uses examples from real study
Concludes clearly
model:
A student preparing for an entry test today has two main choices: open a book or watch a video lecture. Many students prefer videos, which feel easier and more lively. Others insist that real learning comes from reading. In my opinion, books remain the better foundation for deep learning, while videos are excellent for explaining difficult ideas and practical skills.

Supporters of books point to depth. A well-written book explains a subject step by step, develops arguments fully and provides examples and exercises. Reading requires concentration, which trains the mind to focus for long periods. Readers also build their vocabulary and writing skills, since they meet well-formed sentences on every page. Published textbooks are usually checked and edited, so their information is often more reliable than random videos.

Supporters of videos point to clarity. Some ideas are much easier to understand when they are shown rather than described: the movement of a wave in physics, the steps of a chemical reaction, or the way to solve a geometry problem. Videos can use animations, diagrams and demonstrations. A good teacher's voice and expressions keep students interested, and a student can pause, rewind and watch again. For students without good teachers nearby, videos bring expert explanations to their phones.

Each method has weaknesses. Watching a video can be passive; students may feel they have understood simply because the explanation seemed clear, without practising themselves. Videos are also full of distractions, with suggestions for unrelated content one click away. Books, on the other hand, can be hard for beginners, especially when the language is difficult, and some students lose motivation when faced with long pages of text.

The best approach depends on the purpose. To understand a difficult concept or learn a practical skill, a short video can be ideal. To build deep knowledge, prepare thoroughly for examinations and develop thinking and language skills, books are still essential. Many successful students combine the two: they watch a video to grasp an idea, then read the textbook chapter and solve its exercises.

In conclusion, videos are powerful tools for explanation, but books provide the depth and discipline that real learning requires. Students learn best when they use videos to open the door and books to explore the room.

prompt: "Friendships made online can be just as real as friendships made face to face."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains how online friendships can be genuine: shared interests, support, long conversations, friendship across distance
Explains their limits: no physical presence, false identities, shallow contact
Mentions safety concerns, especially for young people
Discusses what makes any friendship real: trust, honesty, support over time
Concludes clearly
model:
Many young people today have friends they have never met in person: a gamer in another city, a fellow student from an online course, or someone who shares an interest in poetry or astronomy. Some say these friendships are not real. I agree that online friendships can be genuine, but they also have limits and risks that face-to-face friendships do not.

Online friendships can be deep and meaningful. People who share interests can talk for hours, exchange ideas and support each other through difficult times. For students who are shy, live in remote areas or feel different from those around them, online communities can offer understanding that they cannot find locally. Friendships also continue online when people move away; a friend who has gone abroad for studies can remain close through daily messages and video calls.

What makes a friendship real is not where it began but whether it includes trust, honesty and support. If two people have shared their worries, celebrated each other's successes and stayed in touch over years, their friendship is real, whether they met in a classroom or a chat group.

However, online friendships have important limits. Without physical presence, friends cannot help each other in practical ways, such as visiting during illness or helping with a move. Much online contact is also brief and shallow, consisting of likes and short comments rather than true conversation.

There are also serious safety concerns. People online can hide their true identities, ages and intentions. Some pretend to be friends in order to deceive, steal money or exploit young people. Young users should be careful about sharing personal information, photographs or their location, and should never meet an online friend alone without informing their parents.

Face-to-face friendships offer things that screens cannot: shared experiences, physical comfort and the ability to read each other's expressions and feelings. Ideally, online friendships should add to real-life friendships rather than replacing them.

In conclusion, online friendships can be just as real as face-to-face ones when they are built on honesty and lasting support. But young people should approach them with care, and remember that the friends who can sit beside them are also precious.

prompt: Should voluntary community service be made compulsory for college students?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words giving your answer. Present arguments on both sides and make your own view clear.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains benefits: empathy, responsibility, practical skills, contact with different communities, help for society
Explains objections: 'compulsory volunteering' is a contradiction, time pressure, risk of a box-ticking exercise
Gives examples of suitable service, such as tutoring, tree planting, hospital help or clean-up drives
Suggests how a scheme could be designed to be meaningful
Concludes clearly
model:
During floods, heatwaves and other emergencies, groups of young volunteers in Pakistan have often been among the first to help, distributing food, water and medicines. Their work shows how much young people can contribute. Some suggest that community service should be compulsory for college students. I agree, provided the scheme is flexible and meaningful rather than a formality.

Community service benefits students in many ways. It brings them into contact with people whose lives are very different from their own, building empathy and gratitude. Teaching children in a poor neighbourhood, helping patients find their way in a hospital or cleaning a local park teaches responsibility and teamwork. Students also gain practical skills, such as organising events, communicating with the public and solving problems, which help them in their studies and future jobs.

Society benefits too. Many communities need help that young people can give: tutoring, awareness campaigns about health or hygiene, tree planting and caring for elderly people. Even a few hours a month from thousands of students could make a real difference.

There are reasonable objections. Some argue that volunteering must be voluntary; forcing students to do it may make them resentful and turn service into a chore. Intermediate students already face heavy workloads and examination pressure, so extra obligations may be unwelcome. There is also a risk that students will simply collect certificates without doing real work, or that colleges will organise poorly planned activities.

These concerns can be addressed through careful design. The requirement could be modest, such as a set number of hours over a year, spread across holidays and weekends. Students could choose from a range of activities that match their interests, from teaching and health awareness to environmental projects. Colleges should partner with trusted organisations and supervise the work properly. Students could write a short reflection on what they learnt, so that the experience becomes a real lesson rather than a box to tick.

In conclusion, compulsory community service, if well planned, would help students grow into responsible and caring citizens while supporting the communities around them. The requirement may begin as an obligation, but for many students it could become a lifelong habit of service.

prompt: Should people be encouraged to walk or cycle for short journeys instead of using motorbikes and cars?
task: Write an essay of about 300-400 words answering this question. Consider both sides and support your view with reasons and examples.
points: Gives a clear answer
Explains health benefits: exercise, weight control, heart health, mood
Explains wider benefits: less traffic, cleaner air, lower fuel costs
Recognises obstacles: heat, unsafe roads, lack of footpaths or cycle lanes, distance, safety for women and children
Suggests what cities and individuals could do to make walking and cycling practical
Concludes clearly
model:
In many Pakistani neighbourhoods, people take a motorbike or car even to buy bread from a shop around the corner. Walking or cycling has come to seem old-fashioned or inconvenient. Yet for short journeys, these simple options offer real benefits. I believe people should be encouraged to walk or cycle where it is safe and practical.

The health benefits are clear. Many people today lead inactive lives, sitting at desks, in vehicles and in front of screens. Walking or cycling even a short distance every day strengthens the heart, helps control weight and reduces the risk of diseases such as diabetes. Physical activity also improves mood and reduces stress. A daily walk to the market or mosque is an easy way to build exercise into a busy routine.

There are also wider benefits. Every short trip made on foot or by bicycle means one less vehicle on the road, reducing traffic jams and air pollution. Families save money on fuel and vehicle maintenance, which matters when prices are high. Streets with more pedestrians also feel livelier and often safer, as more people are around.

However, there are real obstacles. Summer heat in many cities makes walking uncomfortable for much of the day. Many roads have no proper footpaths, or footpaths are blocked by parked vehicles and shop goods. Cycling in heavy traffic can be dangerous without cycle lanes. Women and children may not feel safe walking alone in some areas, and elderly people or those carrying heavy shopping may find walking difficult.

These obstacles show what needs to change. City authorities can build and clear footpaths, plant shade trees along roads and create safe cycle lanes on main routes. Better street lighting would make walking safer in the evenings. Schools could encourage children who live nearby to walk together in groups. Individuals can start with small steps, such as walking to nearby shops in the cooler hours of the morning or evening.

In conclusion, walking and cycling for short journeys benefit both health and the environment, and they should be encouraged. For this to work, cities must make streets safer and more comfortable, and people must be willing to leave their vehicles at home for short trips.

prompt: "Old buildings in our cities should be preserved, even when replacing them with modern ones would be cheaper and more useful."
task: Do you agree or disagree? Write an essay of about 300-400 words, supporting your view with reasons and examples.
points: States a clear position
Explains the value of old buildings: history, identity, craftsmanship, tourism and education
Explains the case for replacement: safety, space, modern facilities, cost, the needs of growing cities
Distinguishes between buildings of real historic value and ordinary old structures
Suggests solutions such as restoration, new uses for old buildings and protection laws
Concludes clearly
model:
The old quarters of cities such as Lahore, Peshawar and Multan contain havelis with carved wooden balconies, colonial-era buildings and narrow streets that have stood for generations. Many are crumbling, and developers often want to replace them with shopping plazas and apartment blocks. Should they be preserved? I agree that buildings of real historic value should be protected, even at extra cost, though not every old structure can be saved.

Old buildings carry history and identity. They show how earlier generations lived, worked and worshipped, and they connect a city's present with its past. Their carved woodwork, tiles, brickwork and architectural styles reflect skills that are rarely practised today. Once such buildings are demolished, they cannot be replaced; a copy is never the same as the original.

Historic buildings also bring practical benefits. They attract tourists, both local and foreign, who spend money in nearby shops, restaurants and guest houses. They provide students and researchers with living examples of history and architecture. A city that keeps its heritage has a character that new buildings alone cannot create.

However, there are strong arguments for replacement. Many old buildings are unsafe, with weak structures that could collapse during an earthquake or heavy rain. They may lack proper plumbing, wiring and fire safety. Growing cities need space for housing, shops and offices, and modern buildings can serve far more people on the same land. Restoration is often expensive, and owners may not be able to afford it.

The answer is to distinguish carefully. Buildings of genuine historic or architectural importance should be identified and protected by law, with help from the government for their repair. Ordinary old structures with little historic value can be replaced when necessary, as long as new buildings respect the character of the area.

Old buildings can also be given new uses. A restored haveli can become a museum, a hotel, a restaurant or a cultural centre, earning money to pay for its own upkeep. Some cities have already shown how restoration can revive old neighbourhoods.

In conclusion, historic buildings are treasures that deserve protection even when replacement would be cheaper. With careful selection, legal protection and creative new uses, cities can grow without losing their past.

prompt: Think of a day when the electricity went out for many hours and your family had to manage without it.
task: Write a narrative of about 250-350 words in the first person. Tell the events of that day in order and show what the day taught you about your family.
points: Opens in the moment the power fails, with sound, heat or darkness
Follows the day in a clear order from morning to night

The ceiling fan slowed, groaned and stopped just as Ammi lifted the pressure cooker off the stove. It was eleven in the morning in June, and the whole of our street in Gujranwala went silent at once.

At first we treated it like an ordinary load-shedding hour. My younger brother Hamza opened the fridge to "save the ice", Abbu checked the UPS, which beeped twice and died, and I sat on the stairs refreshing my phone until the battery dropped to twelve per cent. By two o'clock the transformer on the corner had a crowd of neighbours under it, and someone from the electricity office said it would take "until evening, maybe".

The afternoon was the hardest part. The rooms grew so hot that we carried charpais into the courtyard under the neem tree. Hamza complained loudly. I complained silently, which was worse. Then Dadi, who had said almost nothing all day, asked me to fetch the old hand fan from the steel trunk. While she fanned herself, she began telling us about summers in her village, when the only cold thing in the house was a clay pitcher wrapped in wet cloth.

"We used to wait for the evening breeze like a guest," she said. Hamza stopped sulking and asked how they slept. Abbu laughed and admitted he had slept on the roof until he was fifteen. Ammi brought out the cooled daal and rotis, and we ate in the courtyard, passing one torch between us like a microphone.

The lights came back at half past nine. The fans roared, the television switched itself on and everyone hurried indoors. I stayed outside a moment longer.

I had expected to remember that day as the day nothing worked. Instead I remember it as the day I heard my grandmother's childhood for the first time. We live in the same house, yet it took ten hours of darkness for us to actually sit together and listen.

prompt: Describe a journey by train, bus or road that did not go as planned.

The Tezgam was supposed to leave Rawalpindi at half past seven in the morning. My cousin Fahad and I had planned every hour of the trip to Lahore: lunch at Jhelum, a nap after Gujrat, and arrival in time for our aunt's mehndi that evening.

The train left forty minutes late, which we expected. What we did not expect was the long, shuddering stop in the middle of the fields beyond Lala Musa. Ten minutes passed, then an hour. A guard walking along the track told us an engine ahead had broken down and that we would wait "until the relief engine comes".

Fahad called his mother three times. I sat with my feet on our suitcase, calculating how many dances we would miss. The carriage grew hot, and a baby two seats away began to cry without stopping.

Then an elderly man opposite us opened a tiffin carrier and offered us parathas. "Travel is like this," he said calmly. "You reach when you reach." His name was Rana Sahib, and he had been taking this route for forty years. He told us about the time floods had kept him on a train for two days, and about the stranger who had shared his blanket that night.

Slowly, the carriage changed. Someone produced a thermos of tea. A university student played cricket commentary on his phone for the boys in the next compartment. Fahad, who had been sulking, ended up holding the crying baby while her tired mother drank her tea.

The relief engine arrived after four hours. We reached Lahore at nine at night, sweaty and crumpled, and walked into the mehndi just as the final song began. Our aunt laughed at our faces and pulled us straight into the circle.

I still make plans for every journey, but now I pack an extra packet of biscuits and a little more patience. The most memorable part of that trip was not where we were going, but the strangers we met while we were stuck.

prompt: Write about a time you made a mistake that taught you an important lesson.

The red ink on my chemistry test said 14 out of 50. I folded the paper twice before anyone in the row could see it, but my face had already told them.

It had started three weeks earlier. Our teacher, Sir Naveed, had announced the test on organic reactions, and I had decided I did not need to prepare early. I had done well in the first term, and I believed I could learn everything in the last two nights. So I spent the evenings watching match highlights and helping my friend Usman edit videos for his channel.

Two nights before the test, I opened my notes and found thirty reactions, each with conditions and products I barely recognised. I stayed up until three, drank too much tea, and fell asleep with the book on my chest. The next night the electricity went, and my phone torch died at midnight. I walked into the test tired, confused and pretending to be confident.

After class, Sir Naveed called me to his desk. I expected anger. Instead he asked quietly, "When did you start revising?" I wanted to blame the load-shedding, but I told him the truth. He nodded and said, "Talent gets you started. Habits get you finished."

That evening I made a simple timetable: forty minutes of chemistry every day, a short self-test every Sunday, and match highlights only after both were done. It felt boring at first. By the end of the month, though, I could write the reactions without looking, and the retest came back with 41.

The mark was not the real lesson. The lesson was that confidence without preparation is just a gamble, and I had bet my own future on it. Now, whenever I feel sure I can "manage later", I remember the red 14 and open my notes that day.

prompt: Describe a time when you had to choose between what your friends wanted and what you believed was right.

"Just send the photo. Everyone else has," Sana whispered, holding her phone under the desk.

It was the night before our final English paper, and someone had shared what looked like the question paper in our class group. By the time I saw it, forty messages had appeared beneath it: laughing faces, thank-yous, and plans to "just memorise the essay". My best friends, Sana and Maryam, had already written their answers.

I stared at the blurry picture for a long time. Part of me wanted to look. I had worked hard all year, but English was my weakest subject, and my father had told everyone at the dinner table that I would get an A. Another part of me remembered my mother marking papers at the kitchen table for her own students, sighing whenever she found copied work.

"If it's fake, you lose nothing," Maryam texted. "If it's real, you lose everything by not looking."

I turned the phone face down and opened my essay notes instead. I did not sleep well. At school the next morning, Sana asked whether I had seen it. When I said no, she rolled her eyes and walked away to sit with the others.

The paper turned out to be completely different. The leaked picture had been from another board's old exam. Half the class came out pale and silent. I had not done brilliantly, but I had written about a topic I had practised, in my own words.

Sana did not speak to me for two days. On the third, she sat beside me at break and said, "You were annoying, but you were right." We laughed, though both of us knew it had been close.

The paper's being fake was luck. Refusing to look was not. I learned that the hardest choices are the small, quiet ones made alone at night, with nobody watching except yourself.

prompt: Write about a time you helped someone who was in difficulty.

The old woman was standing at the edge of Murree Road with a plastic bag in each hand, watching the traffic as if it were a river she could not swim.

I was on my way back from the academy in Saddar, tired and thinking only about dinner. Cars, wagons and motorbikes rushed past her without slowing. She stepped forward, then back. A rickshaw horn made her drop one bag, and oranges rolled into the gutter.

For a second I hesitated. I was not sure she would want help from a stranger, and I worried about looking foolish. Then one orange rolled to my shoe, and that decided it. I picked it up, then the others, and put them back in her bag.

"Amma ji, where are you going?" I asked.

"To the hospital on the other side," she said. "My son is admitted. I came on the wagon but I don't know these roads." Her voice was steady, but her hands were shaking.

I took both bags, held her arm and waited for a gap. When a traffic warden noticed us, he raised his hand and stopped the cars, and we crossed slowly together. On the far side, I asked which ward her son was in. She showed me a crumpled slip of paper, so I walked her through the gate, past the crowded reception, up to the second floor.

Her son was sitting up in bed with a bandaged leg. When he saw his mother, he tried to stand, and she scolded him like a schoolboy. Then she turned to me and insisted I take two oranges. I tried to refuse; she would not hear of it.

I was forty minutes late home and my mother wanted an explanation. When I gave it, she said nothing, but she put extra salan on my plate.

The help I gave took less than an hour. What stayed with me was how close I came to walking past. Now, when I notice someone struggling, I try not to wait for an orange to roll to my feet.

Within minutes the street was full of Qureshis. Uncle Javed ran towards the main road. The older cousins checked the empty plot behind the mosque. Zainab's grandfather, who walked with a stick, went slowly from door to door asking the neighbours. Zainab followed him, holding his hand and trying not to cry.

"He came in by himself," she said. "I thought perhaps Allah had sent me a guest for Eid."

Zainab's grandfather looked at the lonely little courtyard, then at Zainab. Something passed between them without words.

The next afternoon, after the prayers, the Qureshis carried a large dish of food down the lane, and Mrs Bano joined them for the meal, sitting beside Zainab. Moti had gone back home on his rope, but from that Eid on, the Qureshis made sure that one door in the lane was always open for her.

On the first day of college I walked confidently into Room 12, sat in the second row and opened my new physics notebook. The lecturer wrote "Introduction to Fine Arts" on the board.

She handed everyone a sheet of paper and a charcoal stick. "Draw your hand," she said. "Not the hand you think you have. The one in front of you." I had not drawn anything since primary school, when I coloured mountains brown and the sky blue. My first lines were stiff and wrong. Miss Rubina stopped beside me, looked at the drawing and said, "You're looking at the paper. Look at your hand." I tried again, and slowly the knuckles and wrinkles appeared.

When the class ended, I explained my mistake. She laughed. "Physics will still be there tomorrow," she said. "Come on Thursday if you like. Art is free for anyone who turns up."

I went on Thursday, and the Thursday after that. My parents thought it was a waste of time at first, especially my father, who wanted me to be an engineer. I kept going to physics too, and I did well, but the Thursday class became the part of the week I looked forward to most. Three years later, I chose architecture, a subject that needed both maths and drawing. My daughter Hira had told me nothing except that I must come. "Just come, Abbu," she had said. "Don't ask." I sat near the back, on a plastic chair that wobbled, beside mothers taking photographs and a grandfather who kept falling asleep.

I drew the camera icon with a big cross. We practised with my phone calling his, over and over. Each time he got it right, I clapped, and he pretended to be annoyed but smiled under his moustache.

On the fifth evening, my uncle called. Dada Jan looked at the notebook, then at the phone, and pressed green. My uncle's face appeared on the screen, with his children crowding behind him. "Assalam-o-Alaikum!" my grandfather shouted, as if he were calling across the sea without the phone.

They talked for forty minutes. Afterwards, Dada Jan put the phone down carefully and said, "Now teach me how to send a voice message."

My mother had pressed my uniform twice and packed me an egg sandwich. My father dropped me at the gate and said, "Be yourself." It was not helpful advice. I wasn't sure who myself was in a place like this.

The first lecture was physics, in a hall with rows of wooden benches rising towards the back. I sat in the middle and kept my head down. My cousin Salman woke me at four in the morning in our grandmother's house in Skardu. "If we want to see the sunrise from the ridge, we leave now," he whispered. I groaned, put on two sweaters and followed him out into the freezing dark.

The path began behind the village, between stone walls and apricot trees whose branches were bare. Our torches lit only a small circle of ground. Salman walked quickly, sure of every rock, while I stumbled behind him. My breath came out in clouds, and the cold air made my chest hurt.

After an hour, the path became steeper and rougher. I had to use my hands on some of the rocks. Twice I wanted to give up. "How much further?" I asked. Salman laughed. "Everyone asks that. The answer is always 'a little'."

Just as the sky began to turn grey, we met an old shepherd coming down with his goats. He wore a woollen cap and carried a stick taller than himself. He stopped and spoke to Salman in Balti, then looked at me and smiled. "He says the city boy is slow but stubborn," Salman translated. "He says that's good enough."

We reached the ridge with minutes to spare. Below us lay the whole valley: the wide, grey Indus, sand dunes along its banks, the town still in shadow. Then the sun came over the peaks to the east, and the snow on the mountains turned gold, then pink, then dazzling white. I forgot that I was tired. I forgot that my fingers were numb.

We sat on a flat rock and ate the dry bread and apricots Salman had brought. Neither of us spoke for a long time.

On the way down, my legs shook, but I felt lighter. I had climbed something I thought was too hard, slowly and stubbornly, and the view at the top had been worth every step.

"Promise you'll come," my little sister Iqra said, holding out her smallest finger. "Promise."

She was eight, and she had been chosen to recite a poem at her school's annual function in Bahawalnagar. Our parents would be at a wedding in another city that day, so I was the only family member who could attend. I hooked my finger around hers and said, "Promise."

The function was at eleven on a Saturday. On Friday night, my friends invited me to play in a cricket tournament the next morning. It was supposed to finish by ten. I told myself I could do both easily.

The match started late. Then it went to a super over. By the time I checked my phone, it was half past eleven, and there were six missed calls from Iqra's teacher's number. I jumped on my bicycle and pedalled as fast as I could, but when I reached the school, the children were already coming out with their certificates.

Iqra was sitting on a bench with her teacher. She didn't run to me. She just looked at me with red eyes and said, "Everyone's brother came."

I tried to explain, but every word sounded like an excuse. On the way home she held my hand, but she didn't speak. That night, I heard her telling our mother on the phone, "He forgot me."

I hadn't forgotten. That was the worst part. I had remembered, and I had chosen something else anyway, thinking I could have everything.

The next day, I asked Iqra to recite the poem just for me. At first she refused. Then, in the evening, she stood in the courtyard and recited it, all twelve lines, about a sparrow building its nest. I recorded it on my phone and clapped louder than I have ever clapped.

I learned that a promise is not a plan you change when something better comes along. Now, I make fewer promises, and I keep every one.

It had rained all night, and water was still trickling through the pipe. I could see one small grey paw and two terrified eyes. I was on my way to the academy, already late, and my first thought was that someone else would deal with it. Then the trickle of water grew stronger, and the crying became desperate.

I dropped my bag and knelt in the mud. The pipe was too narrow for my hand. "Ammi!" I shouted. My mother came out with her dupatta over her head and looked at the pipe. "Get the oil," she said at once.

I ran inside for the cooking oil. Our neighbour, Uncle Khalid, came over too, holding a torch and a flat piece of wood. We poured a little oil around the edge of the pipe. My mother wrapped it in an old towel and warmed some milk. My little brother named it Badal, meaning cloud, because it was grey. I phoned the academy and explained why I was late. My teacher laughed and said it was the most original excuse she had heard all year.

Badal is a fat, lazy cat now and sleeps on top of the fridge. My mother pretends she doesn't like him, but I often catch her saving pieces of chicken for him.

My hands knew what to do before my mind caught up. "Two lines, fluids, cross-match blood," I said to the nurse, Sister Rukhsana, who had worked there for twenty years. She was already doing it. The blood arrived. His pressure rose slowly. At exactly the twenty-second minute, Dr Farooq hurried in, still in his theatre cap, examined him and nodded. "Good work. Theatre, now."

In my first year of college in Faisalabad, our physical education teacher, Sir Kamran, announced that every student had to pass a basic swimming test at the sports complex. I felt sick. I considered asking my father for a medical certificate. I even wrote one in my head.

On the first day at the pool, I stood at the edge while the others jumped in, shouting. The smell of chlorine made my stomach turn. Sir Kamran walked over. "You don't have to swim today," he said quietly. "Just sit on the steps with your feet in."

It took three weeks. There were days I gave up halfway through and went home angry. But on the last Friday, I pushed off from the wall and swam, clumsily, the whole length of the pool. When I reached the other side, I held on to the edge and laughed out loud. Some of my classmates clapped.

The letter was not long. My grandfather wrote about the day I was born, when he had held me in the hospital corridor and promised to teach me chess. He had taught me, a little, before he fell ill. He wrote about his own life: how he had left school at fourteen, worked as a postman for thirty-five years, and read every book he could borrow from the library at night.

"I never went to university," he wrote. "You will. Do not study only to earn. Study to understand. And when you understand, explain it to someone who doesn't."

At the bottom, he had drawn a small chessboard with a few pieces on it. Beneath it he wrote: "White to play and win in three moves. I never finished this puzzle. Finish it for me."

That evening, I found his old wooden chess set in a trunk on the roof. I set up the pieces exactly as he had drawn them. It took me two hours and many wrong attempts, but I found the answer.

I visited Rauf Sahib the next day to thank him. He was very old, and his eyes filled with tears. "He trusted me with the letter," he said. "And I trusted the post." So, in the end, did I.

When our college in Kohat announced a Quran recitation and naat competition for the whole district, I signed up for the naat category for one reason: the prize was a laptop.

I had a decent voice, my friends said, but I had never performed in front of anyone. I was also, I admit, a lazy student who rarely finished what I started. My mother laughed when I told her. "You? Practising every day?"

The first week, I practised for ten minutes a day and thought I was doing well. Then our Islamiat teacher, Qari Sahib, who was training the participants, asked me to recite in front of him. I forgot the words halfway and my voice cracked. He was not unkind. "You know the tune," he said. "You don't yet know the meaning."

So he sat with me after classes and explained each line of the naat: its words about the Holy Prophet (PBUH), his mercy, his patience with the people who opposed him. I began to read the meanings at home in the evenings. Slowly, I started to wake up earlier for Fajr, to practise on the roof while the air was still cool. My mother stopped laughing and began to listen from the stairs.

Three weeks before the competition, I caught a bad cold and lost my voice. I was ready to give up. Qari Sahib told me to rest and keep reading the meanings silently. "The voice will come back," he said. "Make sure the heart is ready when it does."

On the day of the competition, I recited third. My voice was not perfect, but I understood every word I sang, and I could feel the hall listening.

I came third. The laptop went to a boy from Hangu with a beautiful voice. I was disappointed for exactly one evening. Then I realised I was still waking for Fajr, still reading every day, still patient in a way I had never been. It wasn't the prize that mattered; it was who I had become while trying to win it.

I sell corn on the cob from a small cart at the corner of Liberty Market in Lahore. When the clouds come in July, every vendor on the street looks up at the sky with the same face: half hope, half fear.

This morning, the sky was grey but dry. I lit my coals at ten and laid out the cobs in a neat row. By noon, people were buying steadily: office workers, students, a family with three children who argued about who would get the biggest. I rubbed each cob with lemon, salt and red chilli, the way my father taught me. He sold corn on this same corner for twenty years.

At two, the rain began. First a few fat drops that hissed on the coals, then a sudden flood that turned the road into a river. Shoppers ran for the arcades. The clothes vendor next to me threw a plastic sheet over his stall and swore. I pulled my cart under the shop awning and fanned the coals desperately, trying to keep them alive.

For an hour, I sold nothing. I watched the water pour off the edges of the awning and worried about the rent for our room, due on Friday.

Then something happened that always happens, and always surprises me. When the rain slowed to a drizzle, people came back out, cold and damp, and they all wanted something hot. Within twenty minutes there was a queue. A young couple shared a cob under one umbrella. An old man told me corn in the rain reminded him of his village. A girl in a college uniform asked for extra chilli and laughed when her eyes watered.

By seven, I had sold every single cob. I counted the money twice and smiled.

My father used to say, "Rain takes away the customers, then brings them back hungrier." I didn't understand him as a boy. Standing on this wet corner tonight, I understand him perfectly.

On the morning of the inter-school athletics final in Okara, I woke before my alarm and lay in bed listening to my own heartbeat.

I was running the 1,500 metres. A year earlier, I could not have run round our school ground twice without stopping. I had been the slowest girl in my class, the one who walked during PT while the others jogged. Then our games teacher, Miss Samreen, had said something that stuck: "Speed is a gift. Stamina is a choice."

So I chose. Every morning for eleven months, I ran along the canal road near our house before school, at first for ten minutes, then twenty, then forty. My brother cycled beside me with a stopwatch, complaining. My mother made me eat eggs, which I hate.

At the stadium, the heat was already rising off the track by ten o'clock. Twelve girls lined up at the start. Some of them were from schools with proper coaches and spiked shoes. I wore ordinary trainers.

The gun went off. I stayed in the middle of the group for the first two laps, just as Miss Samreen had told me. On the third lap, two girls began to drop back, breathing hard. On the last lap, I could feel my legs burning and my chest tightening. Then I heard my brother's voice from the stands, louder than anyone: "Canal road! Canal road!"

I passed one girl on the final bend, then another on the straight. I crossed the line in second place, three metres behind the winner, and fell onto the grass.

Miss Samreen ran over and knelt beside me. "Second in the district," she said, shaking my shoulder. "The slowest girl in my class."

I did not win gold that day. But I proved something to the girl who used to walk during PT. Every time I face something difficult now, I remember that stamina is a choice, and I make it.

My father had talked about his village near Pind Dadan Khan all my life, but I had never been. "One day," he always said. That day finally came in the winter holidays, when he decided that my sister and I were old enough to understand.

We drove from Islamabad in the early morning. After the motorway, the roads narrowed and the land became dry and rocky, with low brown hills and patches of green wheat. Near the Salt Range, Abbu pointed out the white and pink rocks of the salt mines. "Your grandfather worked there for a while," he said. I had not known that.

The village was smaller than I had imagined: one main street, a mosque with a green dome, a few shops and a row of mud-brick houses with blue doors. As soon as our car stopped, a crowd of children surrounded it. Then an old man came out of a house and called my father by a nickname I had never heard: "Pappu!" My sister and I burst out laughing.

He was my father's uncle, Chacha Ghulam. He took us to the house where my father had grown up. It was now empty and crumbling, but inside one room, my father showed us marks on the wall where he had written his times tables in charcoal as a boy. He touched them gently.

In the evening, we sat around a fire while Chacha Ghulam told stories: how my grandfather had walked twelve kilometres every day to the school in the next village, how he had saved for years to send my father to college in Jhelum, how the whole village had celebrated when my father became an engineer.

That night, I lay awake listening to the wind and the dogs barking far away. I had always thought of myself as a city girl. Now I understood that my life in Islamabad had started here, with a boy writing tables on a wall, and a father who walked twelve kilometres so his son wouldn't have to.
