For the whole of my first year of intermediate in Nowshera, I studied English the same way: I memorised model essays from a guidebook and wrote them out in the exam, word for word.

It worked in class tests, where the topics were predictable. Then came the board exam. The essay topic was "A Rainy Day in My Town". I had memorised "A Rainy Day", but my version was set in a village with buffaloes and a pond. I wrote it anyway, changing a few words. When the result came, my English marks were the lowest in my class.

I was angry with the examiner, then with the guidebook, and finally with myself. My English teacher, Madam Gulnaz, called me to the staffroom. She had read my answer sheet. "Your grammar is fine," she said. "But you weren't writing about your town. You were remembering someone else's."

"Then how do I prepare?" I asked. "I can't guess every topic."

"Stop memorising essays," she said. "Start collecting details."

So I changed my approach. Every evening, I wrote a short paragraph, only five or six sentences, about something I had actually seen that day: the bread seller at the corner, the smell of the river after rain, the noise of the vans at the bus stand. Once a week, Madam Gulnaz read them and circled weak words. At first it felt slow and pointless. After two months, I had a notebook full of real images, and writing no longer frightened me.

In the second-year exam, the topic was "A Visit to a Market". I had never memorised an essay on markets. But I had written about Nowshera's bazaar a dozen times. I wrote quickly and easily, using details nobody else in the hall could have used.

My English mark rose by twenty-two marks. More importantly, I discovered that I enjoyed writing. I learned that when a method fails, working harder at it is not always the answer. Sometimes you need a different method altogether.

In the Abbasi family of Muzaffarabad, every eldest son had joined the army. Hira's great-grandfather, grandfather and father had all worn the uniform. Their photographs hung in a row in the drawing room, three serious men in caps, looking down at every guest.

Hira's brother, Usman, was the eldest son, and he was expected to apply after his intermediate exams. Everyone assumed he would. But Hira, who was a year younger, was the one who stood longest in front of those photographs. She had wanted to be a soldier since she was eight. Usman wanted to study literature.

One evening, Usman confessed it to her on the roof. "I don't want to go," he said. "I'd be terrible. Abbu will be heartbroken."

"Then let me," Hira said. She had been reading for months about women serving as officers in the army. "Why should it only be the eldest son?"

The next day, at dinner, the two of them told their parents together. There was a long silence. Their mother put down her spoon. Their grandfather, who was visiting, frowned deeply. "It has always been the son," he said.

Their father looked from one child to the other. He was not angry; he looked thoughtful. "What do you want, Usman?" he asked. Usman told him. "And you, Hira?" She told him too, steadily, though her heart was racing.

He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Tradition is to serve the country. It never said who must wear the cap."

Their grandfather did not speak to anyone for the rest of the evening. But the next morning, he called Hira to his room and gave her his old army compass. "Learn to read it properly," he said gruffly.

Three years later, a fourth photograph went up on the drawing-room wall, of a young woman in uniform. Below it, on a small shelf, sat Usman's first published poem, framed.

The new family moved into the empty flat opposite ours in Peshawar on a hot afternoon in August. From our balcony, I watched three men carry up a sofa, a fridge and a large wooden box with Pashto writing on it. Then a girl about my age came up the stairs, carrying a cage with a green parrot inside.

Her name, I learned later, was Gul Bano, and her family had moved from a village in Bajaur because her father had found work in the city. At school the next week, she was put in my section. She spoke very little Urdu and sat alone at the back, staring at her book.

At break, some girls whispered about her clothes and her accent. I didn't join in, but I didn't stop them either. That evening, I saw her on the balcony opposite, feeding the parrot and singing to it softly in Pashto. She looked so lonely that I felt guilty.

The next morning, I knocked on her door and offered to walk with her to school. She looked surprised, then nodded. On the way, I pointed out the shops, the bus stop and the shortcut through the park. She told me the parrot's name was Shehzada. I laughed, and so did she.

Over the following weeks, I helped her with Urdu reading in the evenings. In return, she taught me Pashto words, starting with "manana", thank you. My mother sent food to her family; her mother sent back the most delicious kabuli pulao I have ever eaten. Soon our two families were visiting each other every weekend.

By the winter, Gul Bano's Urdu was good enough to read aloud in class. The girls who had whispered about her now asked to sit with her at lunch.

I learned that welcoming someone does not need a grand gesture. It needs one knock on a door. Shehzada still screeches my name every time I visit, which Gul Bano says is the parrot's highest honour.

The road ahead was blocked, and the sun was beginning to set. A landslide had brought down half the mountainside onto the Karakoram Highway, somewhere between Chilas and Gilgit, and a line of buses, trucks and cars stretched back behind us for a kilometre.

My mother, my younger brother Faisal and I were travelling to my uncle's house in Gilgit for my cousin's wedding. Our driver, a quiet man called Sher Ali, switched off the engine and climbed out to talk to the other drivers. When he came back, his face was serious. "The machines can't come until morning," he said. "We'll have to stay the night here."

My mother looked at the darkening mountains and pulled her shawl tighter. There was no village nearby, no hotel, only rocks, the roaring Indus far below, and a cold wind that grew stronger every minute. Faisal, who was eleven, began asking whether there were wolves.

Sher Ali did not seem worried. He walked to a tea stall that had appeared, as if by magic, at the roadside, set up by a man from a nearby hamlet with a kettle and a gas burner. Soon, travellers were gathering around it. A truck driver from Swat lit a small fire with dry branches. A family from Lahore shared their packets of biscuits. Someone produced a rubab and began to play.

As the stars came out, so many that the sky looked white with them, I forgot to be afraid. Faisal fell asleep with his head on my mother's lap. My mother, who had been anxious all evening, laughed at the truck driver's jokes. Sher Ali brought us extra blankets from the boot.

At dawn, the bulldozers arrived and began clearing the road. By ten o'clock, we were moving again. We reached Gilgit in time for the mehndi.

My cousin's wedding was beautiful, but what I remember most is that night on the highway, when a line of strangers became, for a few hours, a village.

I have opened the green gate of this school in Sahiwal every morning for twenty-three years. I know which children arrive early, which arrive late, and which ones try to slip out at break. Today is the last day for the matric class, and I am watching for one boy in particular: Junaid.

He first came through this gate when he was five, holding his mother's hand so tightly that his knuckles were white. He cried every morning for a month. I used to give him a toffee from my pocket and tell him that the gate was magic: it only let in brave boys. He would wipe his face and march in.

When he was nine, he broke his arm falling from the mango tree by the wall. I carried him to the office myself. When he was twelve, he tried to climb the gate to fetch a cricket ball and I scolded him so loudly that the whole street heard. He sulked for a week, then brought me a cup of tea, as an apology.

This morning, the boys arrived in pressed uniforms, laughing too loudly, the way young people do when they are sad. There were photographs, speeches in the hall, and the headmaster's long prayer. I listened from the gate.

At one o'clock, they began to leave. Junaid came last. He is taller than me now, with the beginnings of a moustache. He stopped at the gate and stood there for a moment, saying nothing.

Then he reached into his pocket and held out a toffee. "For you, Chacha," he said. "The gate let me in for ten years. I'm brave enough to go out now."

I laughed, but my eyes were wet, and I had to pretend the sun was in them.

He walked away down the road without looking back, which is how it should be. Tomorrow, a new five-year-old will cry at my gate. I have already bought the toffees.
